utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. For the record, all the accused are here. I think Defence teams, I see a full house today. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, and I can't -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, everyone. Mr. President, we have a new addition to our team, a young lawyer named Christopher Mitchell, who has recently joined the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Welcome, Mr. Mitchell. I think the first thing I need to do -- we need to do this morning is to explain to you, even though you were already aware of what happened, but primarily to the public why we are starting at 10.35 and not at 9.00, as we were scheduled to do. We were all here at 8.00 this morning, but were informed that there was a technical problem with e-court here, which was being attended to. We were being kept updated from time to time. Unfortunately, it's only a few minutes ago that the technicians managed to solve the problem. I wish to thank them for all the efforts they made to make it possible for us to start as soon as we could, but unfortunately we have lost a whole session. We've been discussing, because every minute lost at this particular phase of the trial is crucial, and we were thinking of trying to recover the hour and a half we lost this morning by sitting for an hour and a half this afternoon. From the technicians', interpreters', and reporters' side, I'm informed that they would be available, provided we have an adequate lunch break. I wanted to know if - the courtroom is available, by the way - if there are any problems from the Prosecution or the Defence teams to sit this afternoon. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We're ready to proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the Defence teams has any problems? We hear none, so we'll communicate to you the time when we will reconvene in the afternoon. We just want to make sure that the accused, in particular, and everyone else will have a decent lunch break. Okay. Shall we proceed first with the Kingori exhibits, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We've distributed the tender list. Having -- and I may be putting the cart before the horse, but I figured I'd raise this issue in any event. Having seen the tender lists from my friends, I note that the diary or the notebook of Colonel Kingori, to which he has referred and to which there were certainly specific references on cross-examination, was not listed. I would just offer that as well to the Chamber, if for no other reason than to be able to make sense on the record or based on the record of the document, at least the portions that were referred to during examination. I don't think we need to necessarily enter the whole thing, but certainly the portions that were referred to on cross. Again, that's not necessarily my oar to pull, but I did notice it wasn't on any of the lists. It's 5D00545, and again, for no other purpose than to assist the Court should there be a need to review the actual document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any comments from any of the Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry to start the morning with a sour note, but I wish Mr. Thayer had told me that in the last hour and a half so I could have thought about it, discussed it with Mr. Krgovic, and perhaps with my clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you think first, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd rather not, partly because it's still quite early for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, this is not crucial. Let's deal with the rest of the documents; and after you've had time to think about this, you can make submissions later on at the end of today's sitting. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I oppose the exhibiting of this diary presented by Defence to show the contradictions in what the witness said, so I really don't see why it should be introduced in the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quite follow, basically. I wasn't following you in French, this time, so I am reading the transcript: "I oppose the exhibiting of this diary presented by Defence to show the contradictions in what the witness said, so I don't really see why it should be introduced in the case file." You made use of it to contradict the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your logic that it shouldn't be used in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I did use it actually. I said that it was used only for the impeachment purposes. So my reasons are that this diary was used exclusively by Defence, who are not proposing it to be in the evidence, and only for the impeachment purposes, so I am opposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to reserve our decision on this to later, when you've had time, and that includes Mr. Josse, to think about it if you have any comments. As regards the list itself that was circulated earlier on, are there any objections from any of the Defence teams? None. So all these documents which are listed in the document that was circulated earlier on this morning are being admitted. Then I have a list of documents from the Popovic Defence team. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we do have one objection to the proffering of the debrief of the UNMOs in its entirety. It's our position - I think this is consistent with our prior practice - we've got no problems with the portions of the debrief that were referred to during the cross-examination or even on redirect going in. But to put the entire document in, which is a total of six pages, which contains portions that neither party touched at all and which are completely independent of the subject matter of cross-examination or redirect, I just don't think we need to put the whole thing in. That said, it's not a big deal. I just want to maintain our practice, unless a statement has been made such an issue of so that the entire thing, one side or the other, needs to argue should go in, so that we can have the proper context. This is a circumstance as we do with other witness statements, for example, where we only put in the portions that were referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honours. I showed to the witness this document, but I hadn't time to cross-examine him in full about all contents about this document, and I believe that it is absolutely good foundation to tender this document into evidence. He was -- he was -- these documents was shown to the witness by the other Defence team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We cross-examined him as to what was not in it; and, therefore, in our submission, Mr. Zivanovic is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also used this document during the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other objections in relation to the Popovic list from either Prosecution or other Defence teams? None. Our decision is to admit all four documents; in other words, your objection is being turned down, Mr. Thayer. The only thing is I notice that two of these documents only exist in the B/C/S language, so they will be marked for identification, pending translation. That's, to be precise, is 1D464 and 1D467. The Miletic Defence team, four documents, amongst which also is the one that we've been talking about, the UNMO debriefing. Any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. There is no point in admitting document number 4, which has already been admitted, so the list is restricted to three. Any objections from any of the Defence teams? None. So all these three documents are admitted; however, the third one, 5D214 -- no, an English translation does exist. Okay. So all those documents, these three documents, are admitted. We move to the Borovcanin Defence team list. There are eight documents, some of which have not yet been translated into English. Any objections, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections from any of the other Defence teams? So all these documents are admitted; however, those which have -- which exist only in B/C/S, and the translation at their office is still pending, will remain marked for identification until satisfactorily translated. All right. You will come back to us on the diary, sort of, of Colonel Kingori at the end of today's -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There are two Gvero documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't got the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I think they are objected to, because Mr. Thayer was good enough to notify me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. There are two documents, 5D543 and 6D217. Mr. Thayer. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to the NIOD report, Chapter 4, "Dutch-Bat and the fate of the local population," that is 6D217. I understand from my friend that he now intends to offer the entire chapter, which is approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Section.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- or section of that - thank you, Your Honour - the entire section, which is ten pages in its entirety. Again, we would object to the admission of that entire section, many portions of which or most of which were not touched upon in any form or fashion on cross-examination or on re-examination. I don't think my friend has proffered a sufficient ground or explanation for why he feels the need to move in these additional portions, which are discussed in this section, when none of it was touched upon during the actual examination. Again, it's not just a one- or two-page witness statement or document, it's a considerable section of this chapter, amounting to ten single-spaced pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very simply, there are other parts that we would have put to him, but were unable to, given time constraints, but frankly that's a lesser point. The main point is context. This is a section headed: "Observations and reports by the UNMOs." Bearing in mind those parts that were put to him both by the Gvero Defence and also by the Prosecution in re-examination, we submit that the Trial Chamber should have an opportunity to read the whole of this chapter - it's not that long - simply to see the parts that were put in the proper context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to waste much time on these. I mean, I think over the time -- long time we've been already having this trial, we made it clear that we are all lawyers and judges here. I mean, so a piece of paper, a document, unless it has been really given evidence upon, is never going to substitute the testimony of a person. I mean, so it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I quite agree with the Chamber on that, and I think that's consistent with our feeling, that we trust the Court to be able to make those judgements. I'm just a little concerned about starting a practice. Now, we're about to start the Defence case, so I obviously am thinking carefully about the position I'm taking, but I think our position has been clear with respect to these statements. The next document -- the other section, I do think there are important paragraphs that the Court does need to see to properly place it in context, as opposed to the prior section which I don't believe adds any contextual sense to the portions used in cross-examination. However, this other portion, Chapter 4: "The mood in the enclave," there are several paragraphs that I think the Court should read in order to place that cross-examination in the proper context. Given what, Mr. President, you've just said, I'll stand down in my objection and presume that this entire section will come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I want to say is, notwithstanding that, with respect, we strongly endorse Your Honour's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a basic principle of law that we are all used to. I wouldn't like to waste time on this. Anyway, so these are admitted -- I'm sorry. Are there any other objections from any of the other Defence teams? So these two documents are admitted. Now, before we start with the next witness, Butler, Mr. Haynes, Mr. McCloskey, there are two motions - actually one motion plus an addendum - relating to a request for the addition of a number of documents to the 65 ter list. There were discussions ongoing, taking place in the course of last week. We were told that a kind of an agreement was in the offing, pending finalisation of those discussions. Who is going to update us? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd quite forgotten about that. I'm very sorry. We had resolved it before the end of last week. There were tripartite discussions involving myself, Mr. McCloskey, and Madame Fauveau, and there will be no opposition to that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the addendum?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, neither that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Now, we have, as you know, the witness coming in. We will have a representative of the United States government present, as per our decision of last week, and we will also have a number of, I think three, Defence experts joining the various Defence teams, as per our decisions of - I don't remember when - but a couple of months ago. Yes. I think the best way is to bring in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm sorry. I didn't mean to shut you down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, everyone, Your Honours. I hope a short preliminary. Last night, I informed Defence counsel that we had provided Mr. Butler with certain testimonies from this trial, as our military expert, as we always have before, and I just let them know which ones. Mr. Haynes wrote me back. In fact, we need to go into private session about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There was one other matter that we thought, given the time we've had to discuss it this morning, it would be advisable and courteous to raise with you before Mr. Butler began giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to discuss this in the absence of the US --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can begin that process. I don't mind if that goes on while I'm talking or, indeed, while I wait for them to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I can't anticipate what you're going to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's okay if the experts come in, but it should be discussed in the absence of Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to go over old ground, but you will know that during the course of this case, there have been a number of filings about this witness, his status as an expert, and the sort of evidence he might give, and it followed on from a similar application which was resolved practically in relation to the other main investigator, Jean-Rene Ruez, who gave evidence at the start of the case. Really, I think what we would like to inform you is that we have very much in mind your decision in relation to Richard Butler, and I'll just read it into the record, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Due to the qualifications of an expert, he or she can give opinions and draw conclusions within the confines of his or her expertise." At paragraph 25, you said: "The organisation and general procedures of the Republika Srpska Army is an issue which is relevant to this case. The Trial Chamber finds that Butler's experience renders his opinion on this matter of potential value in assisting the Trial Chamber to understand and/or determine issues in dispute." Now, it is very difficult to anticipate precisely what form Richard Butler's evidence may take in this trial, but we have something of an indication from the reports that he has made, from the testimony that he has given in the two prior Srebrenica trials, and from the proofing notes that we have been provided with in November and very recently. We thought it would be right, rather than, as it were, to surprise anybody by repeated objection, to make it plain at this stage that we will take objection to questioning which seeks to elicit from Richard Butler summary, conclusion, and opinion beyond the confines of his expertise, as determined with this Trial Chamber. I'm going to leave it there, because I know the bat will be taken up by others who have, as it were, the ambit of the opinions he has purported to give in the past. But we lay down the marker now that we will be keeping a very careful eye on what opinions are sought from this witness, and we will objection at every occasion when it seems to us to go beyond the confines of the expertise as found by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think, at this stage, to come up with a broad objection like that it is completely, potentially eviscerates my abilities to put on direct examination. The issues -- Mr. Butler has testified numerous times before Trial Chambers and the Appellate Chamber; and in each case, he has given his viewpoint and analysis on intercepts and what they mean, his viewpoint and analysis on documents and what they mean. He's given his viewpoints and analysis on his intentions of the Muslim army and on his intentions of the Serb army. He's summarised these events to put all of this in context. There's been very particularised issues that he's spoken of. The Defence is on notice of all of those issues. In fact, for example, Mr. Butler evaluated an intercept for the Appellate Chamber that he became aware of afterward, and basically the intercept was exculpatory for General Krstic. The Appellate Chamber took Mr. Butler's viewpoint on that, and it's, I believe, in their finding. So if he's suggesting now that Mr. Butler can't provide the kinds of opinions that he's provided throughout his history - indeed the history of the Srebrenica case - this is outrageous. We have your filing, your ruling, but we -- they had their chance to do this, and if -- they cannot be allowed to pick apart my questioning on things that they have not challenged. I don't intend to do anything more or less, really, than I've done before. I hope -- in fact, I hope it's less, because this Trial Chamber has heard so much more than any other Trial Chamber in the past. I'm not going to be asking Mr. Butler to go through the brigade structures, the corps structures, the main staff structures to find which person is doing what. That material you have heard. But I intend to lead mostly Mr. Butler going through, in chronological order, the documents of this case, some that you've seen, some that you haven't, and try to put them in context with other documents, to give you an idea of what they mean and what he thinks they mean. Also the same thing with the intercept, the kind of analysis that you heard already from Stephanie Frease when she said what she thought an intercept meant. So I don't expect him to make his opinion on whether anyone is guilty or not or go to the fundamental issues of the case, but I don't know what Mr. Haynes is referring to. Of course, we heard this kind of objection with Jean-Rene Ruez, and all I said at that point is we're going to do what we did before and there won't be anything inappropriate about my question or his answers, and we went forward. But I don't know what he's talking about. If he's talking about Butler can't provide his opinion and analysis on documents and intercepts, that is too late in the game, I think, for that issue to be litigated question by question as we go. They've been on notice for years on the fundamental nature of Mr. Butler's testimony and his exhibits, and I don't know what this means, and that's what worries me the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can close the discussion here. We'll take every objection that is raised when it is raised and decide upon it. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this stage, I would like to take just a few minutes, first of all, to support what has been said by my colleague, Peter Haynes, on behalf of his client. But may I recall, Mr. President, that what Mr. McCloskey just mentioned concerning the expected testimony of Mr. Butler, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As we said -- sorry. I don't want you to take it personally, but I think the discussion, insofar as it has been developed, is still in a vacuum, and as I said, we wouldn't like to hear submissions in a vacuum on this. If there are any objections as we proceed, you will have your opportunity to make your objections, and we will decide each objection as it arises and when it arises. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There is one specific issue that I would like to raise, that needs to be raised at this time, before it comes up with Mr. Butler, and this has to do, Mr. President, with the basis of the expected testimony of Mr. Butler. If there is any notice in this case, because Mr. McCloskey says that we have been on notice of the expected testimony and the basis of his testimony, that is incorrect. Much has happened since the Krstic case. Much has happened since the Blagojevic case, and today we out of courtesy take this opportunity to inform Mr. McCloskey of how we will react. But the specific issue I'd like to raise has to do with the basis of Mr. Butler's testimony, and I'd like to use one specific example in this regard. In the proofing notes that we've received concerning Mr. Butler, we have been provided with some conclusions concerning the responsibility of our client, specific conclusions regarding the events which took place in the Zvornik area. Over and above the fact that these conclusions go to the fundamental issues of the case, something just raised by my colleague a few minutes ago, and that we feel these types of conclusions are improper and inadmissible, that we will raise if and when they come up. These conclusions included in the proofing notes were never mentioned before in any of the reports provided to us, which were prepared by Mr. Butler, nor in any of the so-called "narrative" that he has prepared; and, of course, there is a distinction, in our view, between Mr. Butler's reports and Mr. Butler's so-called "narrative." So we were wondering, what was the basis for conclusions that we've been provided for in the proofing notes, which were never mentioned in any reports or narratives. Yesterday, we were provided with an e-mail at 4.00 in the afternoon. This e-mail informed us, for the first time, of some testimony that was provided to Mr. Butler. We can divide the testimony which was provided to Mr. Butler in three categories: Some testimony that he apparently decided to look on his own -- proprio motu he decided to look at some of the testimony; then there was a proofing session; then there was some testimony given to him by the Prosecution; and then yesterday there was further testimony given to Mr. Butler. This testimony, Mr. President, is not all of the testimony in this case. So what we would like to know is: What about the rest of the testimony? Will Mr. Butler's opinion, as an expert in this case, over and above what happens with the objections we may raise, what is the basis for his opinion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Doesn't the same argument apply to the Defence experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it supports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stop here, Mr. Bourgon. If there are -- because, first of all, what is included in the proofing notes doesn't mean that this is the testimony that Mr. Butler will be giving here. We've had abundant proof of that in the past. If there are objections, as I said, we will hear what the submissions are and we will decide from moment to moment, from time to time, as it becomes necessary. As regards such arguments like the one you've just put, that may become a submission later on as to how much weight we should give to the testimony of Mr. Butler, considering what evidence was available to him at the time he started giving evidence. So I think we can stop the discussion here, please, and we'll start with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one further issue I'd like to raise at this time, and it won't take much time. But some of the testimony that Mr. Butler refers to, Mr. President, is testimony that was heard in previous cases; that is, not before this Trial Chamber. This is also one area where we will objection, because we do not know what the basis of Mr. Butler's testimony is and what material he has reviewed in order to draw his conclusion. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why you have the right to cross-examine the witness. Mr. McCloskey, please sit down, and let's get going. First - Madam Usher, one moment - we've got additions. Could you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SCHILDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Heather Schildge, and I'm the legal counsellor at the United States Embassy in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Madam, and welcome. Mr. Lazarevic, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Your Honours. Here by my side is Mr. Djordje Trifunovic, our expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and welcome, Mr. Trifunovic. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have General Slobodan Kosovac. He's our military expert and he is together with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome, General. Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The gentleman at our table is Admiral Bosko Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome, Admiral. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not on those topics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just could you inform Mr. Butler, because I'm obviously not going to have a chance to, if someone asks him a question that calls for a comment about what Witness 168 said, to use this "168" as the term, or I can take a moment and just tell him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can do that in private session. Don't worry. I mean, it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I mean, I just -- yeah. And also Mr. Butler, as has been our habit, will bring in binders of the exhibits that we had planned to go through with him so that he's not limited to what's viewed on e-court, as long as that's all right. That's happened with other witnesses, and that's what he has in front of him. Now, we provided him copies of those documents without any markings on them, and I had asked him, as he's looked at documents that, where time order may be important, to note the time order that he sees, so that we save some time from him having to go to the back of each document to look at"sent" or "receive." So he may, in fact, put some notes about that on these documents, which everyone should have a right to see if he does so. I've asked him to do that to save time. I don't think he's done it yet; but I think over the next day or two, he will be doing that. So, if we could ask him, as he goes along, if he's done that and if people want to see that. Otherwise, I have assembled the documents in mostly a chronological order, and I'm leaving it to Mr. Butler, on issues where time may be a factor, to write those in. So I just wanted that -- everyone to know that. I've sent something like that in an e-mail to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can admit Mr. Butler to the courtroom, Madam Usher, please. In the meantime, some housekeeping matters. We will have a break of 30 minutes at 12:00 noon, then we start at 12.30 to 2.00, then we'll have an hour's break, and then we'll start at 3.00 and finish at 4.30. Is that okay? This is what I am proposing. Okay. Now, I not privy to everyone's diary, agenda, so I don't know. We have to also check with the witness that he hasn't got any engagements this afternoon or whatever. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The witness is coming in, Your Honour. The Beara Defence teams joins the objections and submissions raised by Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal once more. It's not the first time you're giving evidence. You know what the procedure is. Madam Usher is going to hand you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out loud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us testify to the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. I'll try to dispense of all preliminaries. First of all, we owe you an explanation why we haven't started at 9.00 with you, as expected. We had a technical problem, which I am sure you have been made aware of, and then we had procedural matters to deal with and dispose of. We could only start now. We're trying to recover time lost this morning by sitting extra time this afternoon, so we plan to stop this morning or stop this sitting at 2.00 and then resume at 3.00, then finish at 4.30 and then we continue again tomorrow. I hope you did not have any engagements, prior engagements, for this afternoon and that you will therefore be available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a problem, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. As you know, you have here present a representative of the United States government, as per our decision of last week. I'm also informing you that there are three Defence ex parte experts present here, one of whom is a retired general, the other is a retired admiral. Mr. McCloskey, I think you can safely start. Yes. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We're in open session. May we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go back to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Mr. McCloskey, you can start your direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break will be at 12:00 noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For the record, could you state your full name?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My name is Richard Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was born the 19th of November, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I grew up in the United States. Specifically, I grew up in Miami, Florida.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your present job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Presently, I am an intelligent research specialist, or as we're now referred to, a criminal research officer, with the Human Rights Violators Unit for the US Department of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which is an agency of the Department of Homeland Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you give us just a brief description of what that entails, very brief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My role as a criminal research officer is to support our field investigators as well as US attorneys offices and our own administration lawyers with respect to identifying, prosecuting, and removing, where applicable, individuals who have committed human rights abuses and who are residing in the United States in contravention to the Immigration and Nationality Act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does any of that work involve your knowledge that you learned from the job at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Certainly, the techniques and tactics that we -- that I learned here with respect to dealing with law enforcement are applicable in the United States, and a number of cases that my agency is currently undertaking are derivatives of information that have come from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Shortly, does that in many cases involve false statements that former members of the VRS have made on their immigration applications?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My mic is not working anymore, Your Honours. I object to the form of the question. Thank you. We object to the form of the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It presumes there were false statements in those applications, and I don't know that he's made a conclusion as to each of those applications. I think there may be allegations on some of those applications. But Mr. McCloskey is suggesting that each of the applicants who made those applications, that they were indeed false, and that's a finding that, one, would be held over for a criminal federal court to decide. It has been on some of the cases where Mr. Butler has testified, some of which have found that they were not false statements. Secondly, there were some issues that go to the -- specifically the Department of Immigration and Naturalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, would you like to comment? Why don't you concentrate on what the gentleman is here to testify upon, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can throw in allegations. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's just put "allegations" into that question, and can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in part it does revolve around those types of allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how long have you held that job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I began my employment with the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in February of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what job did you hold before that job and before February 2004?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Prior to that, I was a military analyst with the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For how many years were you with the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My total service with the ICTY was six and a half years: Roughly, four and a half years while I was a member of the United States Army, seconded to the Tribunal, and the remaining two years as a UN civil servant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get into a little more detail of that later, but what -- before coming over to the -- being seconded to the ICTY, to the OTP, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was an all-source intelligent technician with the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now I'm going to ask you to -- we're going to go way back in time a bit to have you describe your military career a bit for us. Let's start when you graduate from high school or secondary school, about age 18, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At that point in time, I enrolled in a local community college in Miami and spent two and a half years at school there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Initially, I was studying marine engineering and marine survey technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened to that field?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At a point in time, particularly after spending several months on an ocean-going tugboat, actually living the life, between finances and a few other things, I decided I wanted to stay on dry land for a while and enlisted into the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what year did you enlist in the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I enlisted in August of 1981, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So about how old were you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Twenty, twenty-one, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you start out as a private, like everyone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe your career in the United States Army? I will try to leave pauses, like we know how to do, so bear with me on that, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As an enlisted soldier, from August of 1981, my initial basic entry training, I tracked, go into the military intelligence career field, as part of my enlistment. So after completing basic training, I went to the initial intelligence analysis course at Fort Huachuca, Arizona, which is standard. My first operational assignment was starting in January of 1982, where I was assigned to a military intelligence group in Europe. I remained there doing analysis, primarily human intelligence, human-related intelligence, from 1982 to 1985. I left that organisation, being promoted to sergeant, and went to the intelligence company of an armoured regiment in Fort Bliss, Texas, where I spent 15 months as a non-commissioned officer, doing intelligence analysis with that organisation. I then transferred to the United States Central Command, which is a major joint headquarters at McDill Air force Base, Florida. It's responsible for the entire Middle-Eastern region, from a US perspective. I spent two years there doing research on then Soviet Army operations in Afghanistan, so I was looking at their military operations from a tactical and operational level. After the completion of that assignment, I was selected for appointment as a warrant officer, went to warrant officer -- the basic course, and the warrant officer intelligence basic course, and successfully graduated those courses. Then as a warrant officer, back to Europe, where I was assigned to work in the all-source production section of the 3rd Infantry Division, Wuerzburg, Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just briefly. Can you tell us what, in the United States Army, a warrant officer is, as opposed to a regular officer, lieutenant, captain, major, that we're used to hearing about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the context of the United States Army, there's long been recognised a need to have officers who can specialise in specific career fields, primarily those technical career fields that the army has a requirement for. Many of those, warrant officers, my counterparts, will be specialised in, for example, the aviation field, where they'll deal strictly with issues related to military aviation. You'll have my counterparts in the ordinance field, where they deal with issues of ammunition, or logistics, or things of that nature. In my particular career field, myself and my counterpart warrant officers deal with the technical issues of intelligence, where we are actually the people who conduct those -- that type of detailed analysis. Regular officers in those same fields are -- obviously they have, you know, they have an education level as well. But as a result of their job functions, they do not get into the same technical details that we, as warrant officers, are trained and expected to do. Conversely, those officers have a much more varied career field that they're expected to adhere to. Those regular army officers, for example, may be directed to spend three years teaching at universities, military education there. They will be directed to do other things not necessarily related to the branch that they specialise, that the army requires them to do as part of their professional education and their professional opportunities. So it is a differential that the army uses for those officers who will remain for their careers doing these technical issues and officers who will be broader generalists, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to where you left off. You're a -- you're a warrant officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one thing to be clear on my part, Mr. McCloskey. What would be a human intelligence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's a couple of different kinds of intelligence which we're about to get to, but I do appreciate questions, because I have organised this in a manner where I've tried to -- I've left out things that I may have talked about before, because you have heard so much. So as questions come, I appreciate them. So thank you for that and we'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Mr. Butler, you're now a warrant officer, and you've mentioned human intelligence, so it's a good time to talk about. What kind of intelligence were you looking at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Human intelligence, within the general parlance of intelligence disciplines, is defined as intelligence and information that is derived from human sources, not technical sources. That would, for example, include an overt debriefing or an interview of somebody who might have information. It would include, obviously, information that was derived from clandestine or covert sources of information. It generally encompasses what's known as open-source information, intelligence or information that might be derived from the media sources. Any form of information that falls under the broader rubric of human contact is known in the intelligence disciplines as "human intelligence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about if you got a hold of some orders, orders or documents or reports from the enemy, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That falls into a category of document exploitation, which is also under the broader category of human intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How else have -- has your profession divided intelligence? What other kind of intelligence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Another major branch of intelligence is what's known as "signals intelligence." It is the intelligence information derived from radios or other forms of emitters. There is communications intelligence, which specifically deals with the intercept of radio traffic. There is what's known as non-communications intelligence, which is intelligence that is derived from other broadcast means that don't involve communications; for example, radar, or, for example, telemetry, or things of that nature. So that is the general, you know, types of intelligence related to signals intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Anything else in particular, especially that may be relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The next discipline would be imagery intelligence, which is the category of collecting intelligence information from imagery video sources, and it could be from something simple like hand-held photography all the way up to, of course, imagery derived from reconnaissance platforms or satellites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't obviously want to get into the detail of this, but have you had experience, in your long career, of actually dealing with this sort of intelligence in real-life situations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, with all three branches. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe for us briefly now the kinds of learning and educational experience you had throughout your career so we can get an idea of your training and your education?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As an enlisted soldier, as I've said, I've attended the basic intelligence analyst course, non-commissioned officers academies related to that advanced education for both my leadership skills as well as my intelligence skills. In 1988, when I was appointed for warrant officer, I attended again not only their warrant officer leadership academy for leadership skills, but also the military intelligence warrant officer basic course, where we were given additional training with respect to dealing with the types of intelligence that I've just discussed. Continuing on my career as a warrant officer, when I achieved a specific rank, in my case Chief Warrant Officer 3, a senior-grade intelligence warrant officer, I was required to go back and complete what's known as the warrant officer advanced course, which is less in that case given information with respect to teaching specific skills. But at that point of our careers, where we're considered to be, you know, significant career professionals, it was more of a forum where other warrant officers were brought in for these various course works and it allowed, in a collaborative environment, for all of us to share the ideas and the information and the techniques that we had learned through the years for the benefit of not only that class but, in many cases, the information would be put out to the services as well. So that's the limit of my military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, how about general university education? Have you received any university degrees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have. I have a bachelor's degree from the University of Maryland, their European division, in political science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive that while you were an active service person in the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did, a compilation of a lot of years of night school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Did the US pay for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: They paid 75 per cent, and I paid 25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Generous. All right. Now, you have, in your reports, defined three subject areas of military analysis for land warfare. Can you briefly tell us what each of those are and, as you have before, just encapsulate what they are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the three areas of intelligence analysis with respect to land warfare, they parallel, of course, the three levels of land warfare. The first one is what is referred to generally as the tactical level. "Tactics," as the name implies, deals primarily with issues related to close combat, military operations that last from, you know, the immediacy until 24 to 48 hours. This type of combat is generally described as the type of combat that small formations would be involved in, platoons, companies, battalions, even brigades involved in tactic-level operations. The next level of operations, and they'll be some overlap here obviously, is what is known as the operational level of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you briefly? I know different armies use different terminologies for their forces. Can you briefly tell us, at the tactical level, where in your -- what sort of units in the VRS context are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As an example, there will be orders with respect to Srebrenica that we will see. Those will be actual attack orders or actual orders where the roles of companies and battalions are outlined. That would be an example of a tactical order, having to deal with the particular movement or issues of a company or a battalion or what it's to be doing within the next 12 to 24 hours. So we'll see that in that particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. After tactical was what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The operational level of war deals with the higher military formations; and, again, brigades are involved in this to some extent, division-level commands where various military forces will have them, or corps-level commands. This is the warfare and the planning and the process of warfare that deals more specifically, not with those day-to-day-related issues, but with those issues that generally in combat will transpire between the 72-hour to 96-hour to beyond, you know, several days afterwards. In the United States, you know, when you're thinking of the operational level, you're already thinking beyond the current battle and that you're now looking towards the next battle. Maybe to proceed with the question, where we would be looking in this context, for example, would be where the Srebrenica operation is going on, and at the point in time that people start thinking about what happens after Srebrenica, what's the next military operation, in this case Zepa, and that's an example of now delving into the operational art of war. You're already thinking beyond your immediate battle, and you're now thinking what happens in the next phase, the next part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The third part?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The third part is what's known as the strategic battle, and as the name implies, again, what you're talking here is the overall conflict capacity of an army and how it's tied into a nation. The strategic level of warfare, for example, you know, will encompass not only the actual combat, it will encompass issues related to the development of weapons systems, the development of national strategy or policy on issues. It will encompass issues related to short- and long-term personnel mobilisation: How will the military be financed, how will it be supported, what is its training base, how do you train your current generation of officers, and how do you train your next generation of officers. So that is -- the interrelationships between the three, but, you know, each particular aspect of that, you know, deals with a various component of how a country or nation wages armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, can you give us a short VRS or RS example of what may fit into that category?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: For example, many of -- some of the documents that I'll talk about in the future relate to what are known as operational directives. Now, while they were in fact named "operational," what those directives do, you know, outlines the strategic concept of how the war is to be fought during various stages of the conflict. It melds the military situation on the ground with the political situation within the Republika Srpska, as well as the other warring parties. It also talks about and wraps in the political and diplomatic issues related to the European Community as they involve the conflict in Bosnia. So those types of directives would be an example of what I would call the strategic conduct of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in your experience as a United States Army warrant officer, have you dealt with all three levels?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to your movement over to the OTP of the ICTY. Can you remind us again what year that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That was April of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you said, you were seconded from the United States. Can you briefly tell us, what was the understanding between the United States and the OTP at that point? How was it that you ended up being an OTP person but staying in the United States Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: To start that off, at the time I was an intelligence warrant officer with what's known as the United States 3rd Army, which is the army component of Central Command, and in that place I was for five years doing strategic and operational intelligence. The United States government had agreed apparently to a request from the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor to second, as the practice used to be back then, individual -- an individual military analyst to the Office of the Prosecutor to assist them in understanding many of the military aspects of the crime bases they were investigating; not only the United States, I understand other countries were involved in this process as well, volunteering military analysts. As a result, primarily because I had spent five years in the United States and it was time for me to rotate back overseas again, my name came up and I accepted the assignment, came to Europe, and was essentially loaned to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY for my duration of military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was paying you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As an active-duty army officer, I was salaried by the United States government, I was paid by the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Aside from that, did you become a regular worker at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I showed up at 8.00 and left at 7.00 in the evening, like most of the people who were involved in this case. So I was, for all effects, I was a non-paid UN employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you get assigned when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The initial office I was assigned and working out of is what's known as the Military Analysts Team, a group of military officers and analysts who assist the Office of the Prosecutor in various investigations, in understanding military activities related to the crimes that they're investigating. My initial two months there were essentially to read up and become familiar with this particular area, since I've not dealt with issues related to Bosnia for about five years before I came to the Tribunal. After several months, the branch chief of MAT at the time, Peter Nicholson, assigned me to support the Srebrenica investigation which at that time did not have a military analyst.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Essentially, what that meant was that while I was assigned to the MAT for accountability and other personnel-related activity and I worked in that office, my primary focus was to provide military analysis support to the investigators and the lawyers who at that time were investigating the crime base related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you'd mentioned that you had some Bosnia experience prior to that. Can you describe any Bosnia or experience from the former Yugoslavia, just to -- in broad terms, of course?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: After finishing up with my assignment in Southwest Asia with US 7th Corps during what is now known, I guess, as the first Gulf War, I reverted back to my original position in 3rd Infantry Division in Wuerzburg, Germany. At that time, it was early 1992; and as part of NATO and part of the Central Army group, there was contingency planning going on with respect to the possibility of NATO forces being deployed to Bosnia in some form or fashion. So from my return in late April of 1992, after leave, being back to the unit in May of 1992, until I rotated out in August of 1992, my focus was catching up and looking at the aspects of the conflict in Bosnia during that short period in order to potentially support a deployment of US military forces, should the decision be made to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again briefly, what kind of information sources did you look at to study up on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Primarily, at that time we were less interested in issues related to the actual combatants, themselves, and more interested in relation to more of the -- more of the boilerplate issues of intelligence, which is identifying various issues related to map holdings, identifying areas which may be potentially suitable for deployment areas, working with the logistics staff a lot to provide them with the information related to existing railroads and things of that nature that might support a potential deployment. We were not engaged in a day-to-day monitoring of the military activities of any of the warring parties, if that's what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any general materials for historical background?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At that time, it would probably be whatever news and media reports were coming out of Yugoslavia. I guess it's a matter of fact at this point that, certainly, when the civil conflict in Bosnia started, it wasn't a primary focus of the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 30-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Butler. We left off and you were -- had just been assigned to the Srebrenica team. Can you describe the tasks that you were assigned and what you basically did in those early months and years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was assigned two specific tasks. The first one was to engage in the study of the military and armed forces apparatus that was believed to be responsible for the crime base, in which case would be the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska, in order to understand their doctrine, how they would have been engaged in operations, things of that nature, how their command-and-control organisation would have worked, how their -- you know, all those fundamentals of how the military would have worked in the concert of that crime base. The second component was to actually do the analysis necessary to identify and place the various military units on the ground at the time that the investigation had determined that crimes had occurred or potential crimes had occurred, you know, in order to start making it to the next step to determine who the leaders in those units were and whether or not they would have any potential criminal culpability for the acts that were being charged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did the first thing you described end up in a particular -- with a particular product?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and in the context of my first product, it's known as the VRS command responsibility report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so what kind of materials did you have access to in those early days to help you sort out the procedures, the rules, the basic command doctrines that were necessary to fulfill that task?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: When I first arrived at the OTP, which is 1997, they had already started to compile a library of former manuals, regulations, rules, and doctrinal aids related to the former Yugoslav National Army, and, of course, those were being translated. So we had that type of information to start with in order to lay out the basic doctrinal framework of what the former JNA looked like, how the former JNA operated, how it was organised, and started to receive documents from the warring parties, which, you know, began to lead me in the direction of believing that, in fact, the Army of Republika Srpska was following along in the same doctrinal, organisational, and behavioral lines as the JNA before it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, those are in the early days. Can we just jump forward just a bit, and I don't want to get into a lot of detail here; but, today, what's your conclusion on that point, the relationship between VRS rules, procedures, doctrine, and those of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: After not only reviewing the documents that the OTP received as part of search warrants, you know, from various military units of the Army of Republika Srpska, but also sitting in with interviews of senior VRS officers and commanders, they all acknowledged that, you know, in fact the officer corps, the tactics and the doctrine of the VRS, did mirror those of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In all senses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There were some minor deviations based on the actual conduct of the armed conflict with respect to maybe terminology or with respect to an area -- particular area of operations that were based on municipality -- municipal boundaries and things of that nature. But issues related to command and control, logistics support, combat doctrine, all of those things remained the same as these officers were taught during their JNA professional service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how would you again describe briefly the quality and completeness of the JNA material that you have had access to over the years?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I can't obviously say I've got a complete listing of everything, because I certainly don't know what I'm missing. I have some ideas. But given the broad variety of material that the OTP has at this juncture, we certainly have a very detailed cross-section of the material that would have represented the reporting, the orders, the doctrine, and the whole characteristic of the type of material that an army produces when it's in the conduct of combat operations. So, I mean, I think we've got a fairly good representation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll get into some of that specific material a bit later, but do you -- you lay out the names, the dates, the titles of all the material you had basically in your command study and your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. I footnote that extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about the second task that you talked about, as you described it, following after identified crime scenes and trying to link units, identify leaders and units? What sorts of materials did you do -- did you look at in that review?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: For that particular task, the most valuable documents were those documents that actually represented the combat orders or reports of the units of the Drina Corps that the OTP either acquired through seizures or through other sources; for example, the documents from the Zvornik Infantry Brigade that the OTP received, the documents from the Bratunac Brigade, the documents that are referred to as the Drina Corps collection. Those documents give a fair accounting of what those particular units were doing on given days and set the foundation for interviews of officers, or soldiers of those units, which then corroborated what they were doing at those locations at those particular times with respect to military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Ministry of Interior or MUP materials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the same way that the military documents laid out that picture, the OTP came into possession of documents from the RS Ministry of the Interior, not only those special police units, but also the public security offices or centres, which formed the exact same picture. They give us the foundation of where these police units were, and that, in large part, has been corroborated by the investigation, interviewing the officers in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about open sources from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the beginning, particularly, open source, you know, played a significant role with respect to understanding the basic foundations of the VRS. There's also what we would call open-source information specific to the crime bases, itself, where various media outlets either associated with the Republika Srpska military or independent media people were videotaping various aspects of the operation. In reviewing those videotapes, you know, you're able to identify key members of the leadership, military equipment, things of that nature, which again tend to flow into the larger picture of what particular military units are on the ground, what their activities that they were engaged in, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find any magazines interesting or important?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Not only did the Army of the Republika Srpska publish their own military magazine for the consumption of the soldiers, to read about what their army was doing, in this particular case the first -- the Zvornik Brigade, and later the Drina Corps took that over, published their own military magazine as well, which on a monthly basis would discuss issues of interest to the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade and later the Drina Corps. That magazine is known as "Drinski Magazine."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about information from the investigation, did you have access to that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I had full access to the investigators as well as all of the facets of the investigation that was going on certainly with respect to interviewing military personnel, interviewing police personnel, things of that nature. So I -- I had full access to all of the materials of the investigation during my time here from 1997 through 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you cite any witness interviews or that kind of information in your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As a -- as a general rule, I do not cite or attribute substantive information to witness interviews, primarily because those are individuals who may one day appear before a Trial Chamber and will be cross-examined. I'm not in a position to -- you know, I don't want to rely on their testimony, in the former of statements, as anything that I might rely on. I do, however, in order to set the proper context of some of the crime bases, for example, a place -- you know, the school at Orahovac or the school at Petkovci, where individuals may have arrived and they depart that location, I will rely on some of the statements or prior testimony of those witnesses merely to establish that a crime base was at that location to provide a framework for the remainder of the military documents or other analysis that I do that will, you know, then places the military unit at the location or in proximity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Over the years, have you drafted different addendums to your report as you were called on to do so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For the requirements of the trial of General Krstic, I had the corps command responsibility report, which was tailored towards his responsibility as a corps commander, and my initial product, which was known as the Srebrenica military narrative, which was the first iteration of my laying out the military units and their association to the crime base. Following that, for the trial of Colonel Blagojevic and Major Jokic, I tailored a product known as the brigade command responsibility report, focusing on their roles and responsibilities with respect to the brigade level of command. And, at the same time, I took that opportunity, based on additional information that the investigation was generating, to revise or, more accurately, update the military narrative that I had authored earlier; and that, of course, was tendered as part of the trial of Colonel Blagojevic and Lieutenant-Colonel Jokic. Also as a part of that, I annexed in a new part of the investigation that was developed, which was military documents related to individuals who were being treated at various medical facilities within the Drina Corps zone and who were subsequently on the missing list, and that was a separate annex to my Srebrenica military narrative, the revised version. Finally, in preparation for this particular set of hearings, I authored what's known as the Main Staff command responsibility report, again dealing with the roles and functions of the Main Staff, in order to set the context for my potential testimonies here as well. However, I did not revise the military narrative that I had at the time. By that juncture, I had already left the OTP and I didn't feel that I was in the position, with respect to my current employment and my time constraints, to significantly revise that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So the investigation and interviews and things continued without you. Had you kept up to date with that -- all that information, like you would have if you'd been a UN person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My -- my current job responsibilities obviously preclude me from, you know, keeping up with the day-to-day activities of the investigation or the proceedings. You know, the US government, from the beginning, you know, of my employment, understood that the Office of the Prosecutor had requested and they had agreed to my continuing to function as an expert on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor for this case. But certainly I have a day job, and I'm not in the position to spend, you know, so many hours a day reviewing this. I would, of course, go over new materials that were being published on the OT -- on the ICTY website with respect to the trial. I have read a number of witness statements relating to this particular trial from the website of the ICTY, and I have been in contact with members of the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to continuing issues of this investigation in preparation for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the process of carrying out your -- the tasks that you've described, did you get involved in field missions, actually going in to the -- into Bosnia or other places with the team?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe the sorts of things that you would go along with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Field missions that I would participate in would be those field missions that would have a direct nexus to my military analytical work; for example, I was part of the field missions that were involved in the seizure of documents from the Krajina Corps, from the Zvornik Brigade, from the Bratunac Brigade, as part of that operation. Initially, I was involved in some of the work in trying to locate potential intercept evidence from the Bosnian Muslim Army, at the time 2 Corps, until a point in time when we handed off investigatively to some of the other investigators and Ms. Stefanie Frease. When we started getting access to military officers of the VRS to be able to interview them, I started to participate in those interviews in order to assist the investigators and whatever lawyers were there with understanding some of the answers of the accused with respect to the context of the JNA, as well as to pose my own questions to either confirm or deny our working thesis at the time that the rules, the regulations, and the procedures of the JNA were, in fact, followed by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you actually question some witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have -- can you give us a rough number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: For the OTP, I probably personally participated in maybe 24, 25, two dozen. I mean, I think there were about three separate missions where I participated in direct interviews. And in those missions where I didn't participate in direct interviews because I had other commitments to do, I certainly read the transcripts of the interviews afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go back just briefly. You've talked about some of the material you relied on from open sources and JNA documents and captured material from the VRS, but you've -- you've just mentioned intercepts. Did you work with intercepted radio conversations that were intercepted by the Bosnian Muslim Army of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about -- about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: What, as a component of my analysis or some background behind --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- how did you first view that, how did you analyse that material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As the material -- or as we became aware that this material existed and that the OTP started gaining possession of it, you know, my view of the material, and I think I've indicated this in other forums before the various Trial Chambers, is I was very skeptical of this information, and certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, again, as a military professional, I could certainly hold open the prospect that, you know, we could be baited into some form of a disinformation campaign; and, certainly, within the context of the crime base, those individuals within 2 Corps, many of whom had lost relatives as a result of Srebrenica, you know, would certainly have motive to want to enhance the evidence, so to speak, with respect to various issues of the crime base. I mean, I was aware of that, and so was the investigative team from square one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your experience as a military intelligence analyst in your prior job, was credibility of intercepts and other documents an issue that you would deal with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Not only intercepts, but all intelligence information. A part of -- a part of being an analyst is being able to not only review the information and figure out what it means, but also being able to judge the credibility and the reliability of the information.
