In doing that, obviously, you know, the implied task is that the analyst had to understand the various methodologies that were used to collect the information. That's the first step in determining whether or not the information that you're receiving is -- whether it's technically feasible to even acquire that information, in the first place, as a role of verifying that the information that you're receiving is at least -- you know, has some form of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what, if anything, did you do to review, look into, and test the reliability of these -- this intercepted material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The first thing that I did, at a time while Ms. Frease and others with language skills were actually going through the material and translating it into a language I could understand, was, you know, I took that opportunity, you know, through the work of the investigators, to familiarise myself with the technical capabilities and the practice that the BiH 2nd Corps had and maintained during the war with respect to their ability to intercept enemy communications; the enemy, in this case, being the VRS communications of the Drina Corps and, to some extent, the Main Staff. At the same time I was doing this, I had access to the documents of the Zvornik Brigade and Bratunac Brigade searches. What I was able to do is, from their communications documents with respect to how their communications systems operated, the schematics of their networks and their general practices that I could divine from the documents, I came to the conclusion that at least from a technical feasibility standpoint, the Bosnian 2nd Corps understood what the target environment was that they were collecting against and that they had the technical feasibility to do that. So the idea that they could collect this material was -- was within the ballpark now. It wasn't something that was completely out of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what else, if anything, did you do to evaluate, to test the credibility of this material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the next step of testing the credibility of the material was to determine whether or not we were in a position to be able to independently verify the context of the intercepts, as we referred to them, against material that arguably, you know, the Bosnian Muslim 2nd Corps people would have no knowledge of, as a way of independently testing that. For example, there are - and I know the Court has heard this, so I won't go into the details, obviously - but there are numbers of documents that were seized from Bosnian Serb Army or VRS headquarters or other locations that refer to times, places, and events that it is unlikely or impossible that the ABiH 2 Corps people could have known about at the time, that these records were being created, unless they'd actually intercepted these communications, pertaining to fuel deliveries, pertaining to various events happening on the ground, things of that nature. So in an intelligence world, having the ability to look at a potential adversary's actual collection of orders and then marry it up with the intelligence that you're collecting in the first place, from an ABiH portion, was definitely a unique -- a unique opportunity to really get an understanding of how good or how bad the ABiH 2 Corps people were in collecting against this particular target environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you able to review interviews of ABiH intercept operators, see their testimony, judge them as individuals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did, primarily in the context of the trials against General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did that factor into your overall view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It -- it certainly reinforced my opinion that the people who were collecting the data, you know, understood the target environment that they were collecting against. They knew what they were doing and had the technical means to do that. Certainly the fact that in most cases the VRS communications was not encrypted certainly lended to their ability to do that. So, again, it just reinforced my opinion that what the OTP was looking at, within the context of the intercepts, was in fact an authentic, you know, contemporaneous version of what they were doing in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you mentioned "disinformation." Has your review of all this material in the investigation shown you any efforts by the VRS to get out disinformation or false information over the airwaves that could have been picked up in these intercepts that you're reviewing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, within the context of disinformation, the thing to note in the fact of disinformation is disinformation is part of a plan. There is a motive behind attempting to deceive or misinform the enemy. Ideally, what you're trying to do is completely draw him, you know, away from what you really intend to do. So disinformation is not -- it's not random. There's actually a planned campaign which does this on a normal basis. When you look at the contextual body of the ABiH intercepts, there certainly was an awareness by many members of the VRS to include their senior commanders, that the communications that they were talking to were not secure. They knew the ABiH had the potential to intercept them. But I don't see evidence of a disinformation campaign where communications disguised as official communications between correspondents in the VRS were being designed to actually draw the attention of the ABiH intelligence personnel to a different part of the battlefield or to a different avenue of what they were actually doing. I mean, their primary concern was to prevent the leakage of information, not to engage in a more sophisticated effort to direct or steer the analysis towards a different conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You have provided us with a recent copy of your CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 681. We have marked the various narratives and command reports also with numbers, and I will provide Your Honours with that list later, not take the time to go over it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did you include in your narrative and your command reports detailed annotations or cites to the materials that you were relying on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are those materials -- how important are those materials to have at hand when reviewing your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I find them personally valuable to have them at hand. One of the fundamental components of my analysis is I try to be as conservative as possible with that particular analysis, and as a result I rely heavily on the documents and what the documents say at face value. I try not to read much in to those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just -- I want to go very briefly to an area, and I don't want to have to use documents about it, but can you tell us, who did you learn was in overall command of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: During what period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, during that period, by law and in reality, the commander of the armed forces, the supreme commander, was Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe who or what made up the armed forces, by law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, by law, the armed forces were made up of two components. One is the Army of the Republika Srpska and the other one is the Ministry of the Interior or the police forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there anything that had to be in place for the police forces to be considered part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the context of post-1993 and going into 1994, the -- a series of laws that were published in the Official Gazette articulated that the police forces would become part of the armed forces when the political decision was made to declare either an imminent state of war or a full state of war existing within the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the period of July 1995, had an imminent state of war been declared?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, an imminent state -- an imminent threat of state of war was declared back in June of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are the documents and laws supporting this all set out in your -- in your reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, another question. In your command report, did you identify what kind of criminal law, if any, was in effect in the Republika Srpska throughout the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: What I was able to find out, one, as a result by analysis, as well as subsequent interviews of personnel, was that the law of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted as the law of Republika Srpska. I think they made it official in December of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we haven't used e-court before. We always had you put things up on the ELMO. So as I mentioned to you, there may be a slight delay. But is this a document you've pointed out for us that supports the conclusion you just made? And, Mr. Butler, you might just open up your binder.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It would be easier for me to read, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As everyone knows, you've got binders that reflect the material in the computer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what are you citing us to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This is a particular law and amendment to the Criminal Code of the SFRY, essentially redesignating it, with minor changes, as the law of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's now go to the next exhibit, 65 ter 424.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is Chapter 20 of the Criminal Law that you have identified; and as it comes up, I will just mention, as we leaf through some of the articles, we see military things like failure or refusal to carry out an order, refusal to accept or use arms, those sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I want to get us to is on page 17 in e-court and page 104 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Article 239, which states, and I'll read it as it's coming up: "A subordinate shall not be punished if he commits a criminal act or by order of a superior officer which relates to official duties, unless the purpose of the order was to commit a war crime or another serious criminal act, or if he knew that the carrying out of the order constituted a criminal offence." Now, this particular crime, do you have any knowledge of whether or not officers trained in the JNA would be aware of -- or been trained on the Criminal Code that was in force in the former Yugoslavia prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Certainly within the context of this article, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As part of the professional development and education of those career JNA officers, there were -- they were required to attend various military academies, military training classes or courses. Interviews with those officers in many respects confirms the fact that the inherent, you know, knowledge relating to their own military laws, as well as, you know, adherence to the broader Geneva Conventions, were topics that were taught at those locations. So as part of their on professional development, these issues were broached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next set of laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Chapter 16. It's 65 ter 411, and it's on page 1 of the e-court, B/C/S page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This chapter is entitled: "Criminal Offences Against Humanity and National Law." I just note on that first page, it has the crime of genocide. I won't read it all out, but it includes, as a potential part of genocide, "forcibly deports the population." Then down in Article 42, "War Crimes Against Civilian Population," it notes an attack on a civilian population as something else, and just another part of it, exposing the population to starvation, confiscation of property. Did these laws have any applicability to the -- your analysis and the crimes you were investigating?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They had applicability, in the sense that, one, the laws themselves were applicable to the Republika Srpska and specifically the members of the army or police of the Republika Srpska; and, two, many of the offences that the Office of the Prosecutor was investigating with respect to Srebrenica would have been encompassed within the described actions here in these laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, would the -- would career officers in the JNA have received training on the Geneva Conventions and the laws as set out in their own laws?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, that's briefly what I'll ask you about on what law you found. Did you find any military guidelines or regulations that actually directed the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska relating to crimes against international law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember, in particular, a set of guidelines? Can you describe that briefly, and then I think we can probably go to it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There are several. But within the context of the former Yugoslav National Army, one of the most valuable documents is the 1988 regulations pertaining to the application of international law and the laws of war on the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll get to those, but was there a document that came out of the Main Staff that talked about the applicability of those regs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, on a number of occasions shortly after the armed conflict began in earnest, both political leadership as well as the military leadership published various aspects of guidance to the various political and military bodies to confirm that, you know, these rules and regulations remained applicable to the VRS, even though they were labelled "SFRY."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter number 28, something that you have cited in your reports and testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, as it's coming up, I will help outline it. It's from the Main Staff, the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 6 October 1992, entitled: "Guidelines for Determining Criteria to Criminal Prosecutions." I'd like you to look at what appears to be a cover letter under the name of Commander Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what can you tell us about this cover letter? What is this referring to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In -- you know, sometime during the summer/early fall of 1992, the military prosecutor office or branch at that time published a 14- to 15-page document which laid out the various aspects of SFRY law and how they pertained to the VRS. In many respects, those, you know, pertain to the law of the arm forces regulating military discipline and procedures with respect to conscript call-ups, mobilisation, failure to follow orders, things of that nature. They also outlined the applicability of international law that was found in the SFRY code to the VRS as well. So the military's prosecutor's office drafted the base document, and what we're looking at now is the cover memorandum that was published by the Main Staff that essentially promulgated this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you been able to make out anything from these initials at the bottom, "SS/MR," on who may have been involved in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what have you come to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The initials "SS," to back up a little bit, is part of the scheme, and I believe the Court has heard this before, the initial set of initials is the person who drafts the memorandum, the slash, and then of course the typist. In this particular instance, the initials "SS" stand for "Savo Sikanovic," who was a member of the VRS Main Staff, specifically Morale Legal, and Religious Affairs branch or sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why do you conclude that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In 1992, at the time this memorandum was published, the military prosecutor's office, the military court system, were under the administration of the VRS. At a later point in the war, those responsibilities were relinquished by the army and, in fact, picked up by the Ministry of Defence. But at the time, the sector under the, you know, direction of Lieutenant-General Gvero was responsible for the administration or setting up the framework of the military prosecutor's office and the military justice system. In that context, the only officer with the initials "SS" would be Colonel Sikanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go into the guidelines themselves, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's at 65 ter 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, they begin by talking about various Criminal Code offences, like failure to call up and those sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I want to skip through that and get to e-court page 7, which is B/C/S page 23 and 25 and 27 as we go through it, but I want to start with paragraph 3, which maybe -- may start on page 25 in the B/C/S. In English, it's page 7 -- oh, 8, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is entitled "Criminal Offences Against Humanity and International Law" pursuant to Chapter 15 of the Criminal Code -- sorry, 16 of the Criminal Code, which is what we just referred to. And, Mr. Butler, looking down the paragraphs, we see references to genocide, Article 141, and the other crimes that we had just gone over in the previous document -- a couple of documents ago. How does this fit into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, it goes to confirm the applicability of that particular section of what is then the SFRY Criminal Code, you know, is being adopted and, you know, will be followed by the VRS as a component of the formation of their new state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't read it out; but the paragraph preceding the mentioning of the different articles, it starts out: "Crimes against humanity and international law ..." I know you've read that many times. Do you have any disagreement with that conclusion, as we all read it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I think it's a fair characterisation of how these things can occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then looking at the paragraph at the bottom of the English page, now I think this goes over to B/C/S page 27, a 27 and then to page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It begins by talking about: "In addition to preventing criminal acts which are in violation of the norms of humane conduct and international law, the Armed Forces of the Army of Republika Srpska are required to abide by the instruction on application of the International Laws of War ..." Is this -- are those the instructions that you had just referred to earlier as being followed by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I want to look at the top of English page 8 and B/C/S page 29 -- English page 9, where it starts -- B/C/S 31, I'm told, from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After the paragraph that states they have to follow the International Laws of War, it states: "From this follows the explicit responsibility of the officer corps of the Army of Republika Srpska as the givers of orders in command of the armed forces, whose members could commit or are committing some of these offences, to take uncompromising action and prevent such conduct. "This responsibility belongs, by its nature, particularly to high-ranking individuals and officials in state, military, or public organisations who are in the concrete circumstances in a position to issue orders." And the next paragraph: "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures to prevent the consequences or the acts themselves and expose perpetrators to criminal prosecution, this in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences." Are you aware of either of these two paragraphs, these guidelines, ever being withdrawn in any order or in any policy of the VRS or the RS at any time during the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also, if we go down a few paragraphs, there's a short comment by the author. It says: "It is noteworthy that officers and units on the front line witness such incidents and quite frequently even take part in them, but make no attempt to prevent such conduct by individuals in a unit," referring to criminal conduct. In your analysis of the evidence, did you see this occur, where officers on the ground didn't do anything to stop it and actually took part in it, themselves, based on orders and other things you've read?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Well, particularly in the context of where this document was written and the time frame, reflecting a well-known problem at the time that many of these smaller units that were organised as military police units or self-styled paramilitaries, that both the troops in them and their soldiers were engaging more in criminal acts than they were in legitimate acts necessary to further the goals of the military forces. Again, the fact placing the obligation on the officers, you know, if the officers are engaging in that type of conduct, themselves, or are at the very least condoning it, the message that the soldiers are going to hear is that this kind of conduct is, in fact, acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 416.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is something you've identified as an order or a law under the name of Radovan Karadzic, 13 May 1992, on the application of Rules of International Law of War in the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is this something you found to support your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to believe this was not a proper enactment of law that was in place at the time of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. This remained in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to that particular JNA regulation that you had referred to and was referred to in one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 409, entitled: "Regulations on the Application of International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of SFRY," dated 1988. Now we're going back into the JNA regs. Can we take a look at I believe it's page 14 of the document, and it should be 14 in e-court, and it may be page B/C/S -- B/C/S page 16, entitled: "Prevention of Violations of the International Laws of War and Criminal Responsibility for War Crimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I just want to point out, and I won't take the time to read them, but you have talked about paragraphs 19 and 20, 19 entitled: "Responsibility of Parties to the Conflict for Violations of the Laws of War"; 20 is entitled: "Personal Responsibility for Violations of the Laws of War." I note in paragraph 20 that talks about personal responsibility. A paragraph or two down, it says: "The perpetrators of such criminal acts may also answer before an international court if such court has been established." Was that old JNA policy? Do you know anything about what the RS policy was in July 1992 about recognising any international court?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, you know, obviously the ICTY did not exist at that juncture. Having said that, the VRS and the RS, you know, explicitly indicated that, you know, these regulations would be in force for them as well. So I guess by default, you know, if a future court had been established, it would have put them on notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what the -- do you have any knowledge about what the RS view was of the ICTY in July 1995? I don't know if I've asked you that before; but if you know, you can answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, I know by -- there is a document floating around, roughly March of 1996, from the Main Staff which reflects that their position is that the ICTY is, of course, illegal and has no authority to do anything there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I won't get into 1996 at this point. All right. Now, the -- do you have any reason to believe that the other paragraphs, paragraphs 21, 22, 23, were rejected or not in existence at the time in 1995 in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to a particular section. I won't go through any more detail on that. That's something you talk about in your narrative or in your command report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 409. It's the same -- it's the same rules, but it's a section on page 60 in the English, entitled: "Prisoners of War."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The part I want to ask you a couple of questions about begin on page, I believe, 64/65 in the English. It's actually paragraph 216 in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, 64 in English. I believe it's page 57 in the B/C/S, entitled: "Personal belongings of Prisoners of War."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't go into it again in the detail, but what does this roughly prohibit, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It reiterates the provisions in the Geneva Conventions and the additional protocols about the fact that individual soldiers who are captured as prisoners of war are entitled to keep their personal property or any military gear with respect to -- that's construed as personal property or needed for the protection of those soldiers, which are normally issues such as uniforms. In a chemical environment, it could include letting the soldier keep a protective mask, potentially letting a soldier keep a helmet. It allows him, you know, any food that he has on his person, identity cards, money, things of that nature, that those things are considered not to be the property of the state. In most respects they are considered to be the individual property of the soldier; and, as such, the soldier should be permitted to retain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can't you take money off a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, at some point, presumably, the detaining power would want to take money off the of the prisoner, but there's also procedures where it's going to be vouchered and properly accounted for. It's not customary procedure to -- for the battlefield soldiers who are capturing this individual to keep the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you been able to identify actually some orders or documents that speak to these issues that we have just talked about and communicate them to the officers or troops of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the first one that you've talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3035. This is on page 1 of the English, and it's from the Command of the Drina Corps, 15 July 1993, entitled "Treatment of Prisoners of War," and the part I'm looking at is the second paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says: "From the moment they are captured, enemy soldiers who are put out of action must be treated as prisoners of war in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. Actions contrary to international and domestic law constitute serious criminal offences. "In addition to criminal responsibility, persons acting in this way also incur all other types of responsibility. This responsibility rests not only with the immediate perpetrators of criminal offences and inhumane treatment, but also by their superior officers, because prisoners of war are not the property of individuals or military units, but the responsibility of Republika Srpska" -- "of the VRS," excuse me, "and the Republika Srpska. "Prisoners should be isolated as soon as possible and put in a safe place. Inhumane and unlawful treatment is extremely harmful to the struggle of our people and must be prevented by all legal means. It should also be borne in mind that we can exchange captured enemy soldiers for our soldiers who have been captured and thus return them to their families." Now, this comes out under the name of Deputy Commander Colonel Milutin Skocajic. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At this time, Colonel Skocajic was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. Given the fact that it's the deputy commander and not Chief of Staff, I'm assuming that, for whatever reason, the corps commander at the time, Milenko Zivanovic, was not available to sign this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this, the paragraph and the document itself, reflect the international law on the documents and the applications that we reviewed previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would this go on to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's addressed to all -- all commands of all brigades, as well as some of the specialty units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 15 July 1993, who was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At that time, it would have been Major Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this comment about "bearing in mind that captured enemy soldiers get exchanged," what are they practically pointing out in that situation, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the strong inference, particularly when you look at the first paragraph, is that a battlefield practice has been developed; whereas, units who are immediately responsible or who are immediately capturing an enemy combatant are taking it within their own responsibility to kill them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: -- or otherwise mistreat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you mistreat a prisoner and then exchange him, does that have any practical knock-on effect, possibly, to prisoners who are in custody of the enemy force?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of practical circumstance, you can assume that if you're mistreating your prisoners and some of those prisoners are ultimately repatriated back to their own foreign -- or their own army, you know, the word's going to get around that their prisoners are being mistreated and you can kind of expect that prisoners from your army, who are being held by them, you know, may very well be subject to the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another practical document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3034, dated 17 July 1993. This is a brigade document from the Bratunac Brigade, in the name of Commander Cvjetin Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this document you talked about, you said, I believe, in the middle of that second big paragraph, It says: "Our former country, SFRJ, incorporates its rules in its criminal legislation. In the present stage of its establishment as a state, the Republika Srpska has adopted the provisions of the criminal legislation of the former SFRJ and, therefore, the provisions of the international conventions." Okay. So, here we have the Bratunac Brigade, and it talks about, again, instruction on the treatment of prisoners of war. I won't go into all of it, but -- so what is this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Pursuant to the 15 July order from the Drina Corps, what you see here is the brigade commander receiving that order and essentially reiterating the content of that order to their particular subordinate formations. In this case - and it's kind of hard to see on this - but certainly where it has "Command," on the original B/C/S version, it's got a blank line. The customary practice was they would then hand write in this particular document where each version of this document would go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where would it go to in a brigade context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It would normally go to the battalions as well as the staff organisations of the brigade itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to ask you a lot of detail about that, that structure. I think the Court has heard quite a bit of the various structures of battalions and brigades and corps and Main Staff. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 697, that you found. It's a Zvornik Brigade document, and I've not found a date on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a bit of a different subject; but in the left-hand corner of it, it says: "I approve, Commander Major Vinko Pandurevic," where it is signed and stamped, but it's in the name of Chief of Staff Captain First Class Dragan Obrenovic. As you pointed out before, the first paragraph states that: "On the basis of provisions of the rules of the brigade, items 114-124 and 125-149, the ..." and then it talks about the rules of the command. Now, what rules is Mr. Pandurevic and Mr. Obrenovic talking about in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: They are talking about the 1984 rules for JNA brigades, be it infantry brigade, motorised brigade, things of that nature, light infantry brigade. So they are referring to a former regulation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So we have now moved away from international law to the rules associated to the functioning of the brigade, and you've already talked briefly about how the army adopted the JNA rules, so I'm not going to ask you about that in general anymore. I want to go in particular to one -- to one of those rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 694. It's a JNA rule dated 1984, entitled: "Brigade Rules for Infantry, Motorised, Mountain, Alpine, Marine, and Light Brigades."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Butler, I want you to go to the section on Command, which I have as page 37 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be B/C/S 63 and 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, particularly 115 states: "The brigade commander has the exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units." What does that mean? What has your investigation and your review of the materials of the VRS, the JNA, and general military practices led you to -- can you just tell us what that means, practically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It is a -- in practical terms, it is a universal tenet, for the most part, within professional military organisations that within the context of the brigade, the brigade commander is, by law and regulation -- he has the exclusive right of command. Individuals from outside that formation, even if they're higher-ranking individuals, do not have the authority to interfere with that particular commander's right to command his own brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It goes on and says: "He bears full responsibility for the work of the brigade, command, and subordinate commands, for the state of morale, for security, combat readiness, for training, and for the proper performance of tasks." Can an outside officer, as you've just said, come in and take over that commander's responsibility for those things?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, just as he has the exclusive right of command, the collateral effect there is he also is the one who ultimately bears responsibility for the actions of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what military process or procedure would have to take place before a brigade commander no longer had command responsibility under these regs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: He'd have to formally be relieved or relinquish command to the superior next in line that's authorised to either relieve him or accept his relief of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It says -- it goes on and says: "The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their fulfillment, and demands their strict execution regardless of difficulties that arise." Can you go through that, one by one, and tell us practically what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It -- in a nutshell, what that particular sentence is is a one-line sentence that reflects what later is known as the command and staff process. The commander takes decisions either independently, on his own, or after consulting with his staff and getting their advice. He assigns a task to units, whether he elects to individually assign a task or whether that task is formalised through orders published by his staff. He monitors their fulfillment, and this is a key issue. A commander does not issue orders in the abstract. As part of a function of command, you know, he's required to verify that those orders are, in fact, being carried out, and he has the right to demand compliance. Again, commander is expected to be able to accomplish his role of command, regardless of whatever difficulties might arise. These regulations are published for people who will command military units in wartime. It is anticipated that there will be many times during the course of an individual's command that the compliance of orders and the carrying out of the mission is going to be difficult because, you know, the enemy forces that you will be facing will be taking every step that they can to try and prevent you from carrying out that function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this last part, I'm talking about decisions and tasks: "... and demands their strict execution, regardless of difficulties that arise." In your review of the documents and the orders, how serious did VRS officers take orders received from their superiors? I mean, VRS professional former JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The trained professional officers, particularly because they were the most educated and held the most senior positions within the army, were well aware of the seriousness and the gravity of orders that were issued and, you know, what they had to do to undertake -- to follow those orders. Even codified under the armed forces law that they were operating, I mean, the ability to follow the orders to the extent necessary, you know, these are major, significant issues to officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the context of Srebrenica, do you see any officers refusing to follow orders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the context of certainly one of the most serious instances, where an officer refuses to follow whether it's an explicit order or whether it's an order given by General Mladic, as we understand it, is on the 16th of July, 1995, when then Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic unilaterally takes a decision effectively authorising a battlefield truce in the area of the Zvornik Brigade to allow the Muslim column to pass through his lines, which was certainly not something that either the Drina Corps or the Main Staff had intended to happen. So that is a major significant instance where Colonel Pandurevic, on his own, with the best interest of his brigade, and based on the decision and his right to command, made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "best interests of the brigade," what do you mean? Why do you think he made it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within, you know, the context of the events that were occurring on the battlefield at the time, several battalions of the Zvornik Brigade, specifically the 4th Battalion and the 6th Battalion, elements of the 7th Battalion, were decisively engaged and frankly quite outnumbered by the sheer size of the Muslim column that was carving their way through Zvornik Brigade territory. By looking at the orders and the reports that are generated by this battlefield truce that Colonel Pandurevic engaged in, it's clear that, you know, he came to the conclusion that continuing to fight the column would not prevent the column from breaking through to the friendly territory of Muslim lines, as they were trying to do, and would only result in additional casualties for his own military forces. So, again, you know, within his authority as a brigade commander, he took it upon himself to, you know, effect a battlefield truce with the enemy to allow this column to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We may get into that a few days down the road when we get to some more documents, but let me also ask you an example related to General Pandurevic. Do you recall, on 11 July, on the video, General Mladic, in the presence of at that time Colonel Pandurevic, making some kind of statement or order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the context of the video scene, General Mladic - and not only the video, but, you know, in larger part other officers have confirmed this accounting of events - as the day was ending, General Mladic was giving his brigade commanders, who had accompanied elements of their brigades into Srebrenica, orders on what he wanted to accomplish next on parts of the terrain. You know, obviously that's an order directly from the army commander. But several of the brigade commanders, in a quick council of war, so to speak, went back to General Mladic and told him that, you know, given the light conditions and everything else, the battlefield situations and the fact that they didn't know where some enemy components was, that tactically speaking they did not think that was a wise move and requested that General Mladic reconsider his decision. In fact, you know, from the accounts of the officers who were involved in that, General Mladic did, in fact, reconsider his position and countermanded his original orders to these commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall what Pandurevic was saying on the video in response to Mladic? If you don't, don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It's been a lot of years since I've seen the video or the transcripts, so I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't mind if you lead him on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Your microphone, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I was just saying I don't mind if Mr. McCloskey puts the words to Mr. Butler, if he knows them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. You've got about four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes has quized me on that. I think it was something about, We've got to get the Browning up on the ridge, there's Muslims up there. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the context that they wanted to -- they wanted to put some form of a heavy machine-gun position and other units up on a ridge. The subordinate -- the brigade commanders, and I think Pandurevic specifically was noting the fact that they had in fact lost contact with the 28th Division. They didn't know where it was, and they didn't particularly feel comfortable putting an isolated element up there, that as the sun was coming down, in an unfamiliar position, could potentially be attacked and ambushed later that evening. Again, it was a, you know, a quick council of war and it made eminently sense militarily not to want to expose themselves, given the fact that they did not have a good idea, from their own reconnaissance, where the bulk of the 28th Infantry Division was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there evidence that Colonel Pandurevic took on Mladic on his 12 July decision to go to Zepa as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So with this evidence that at the time Colonel Pandurevic was willing to take on Mladic on issues that involved the safety of his troops, do you see any evidence of Colonel Pandurevic taking on General Mladic when it came to the commission of violent war crimes against the Muslim army prisoners or population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think -- is it break time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have about two to three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It might be -- well, let me see if I've got one more document. It may not be a two- to three-minute document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break now, as we agreed on earlier this morning. We'll reconvene at 3.00, and then we'll sit right through until 4.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened to the representative of the US government?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you may recall in the motion, they normally just stay during the parts that have to do with Mr. Butler's background, especially when they were part of the US, and then come back when that section is up for cross-examination. But the -- Ms. Schildge did want me to pass on to you that, of course, they are available at any time should some issue come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, no. It's just I noticed her absence, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I just noticed that I needed to go back to this paragraph 115 on the brigade commander. It's in your tab 12. I forgot to ask you about the second -- the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's at 65 ter 694. It should be page 37, in B/C/S page 64. Yeah, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's that second paragraph: "Through his personal conduct, work, involvement, and the implementation of the SKJ policies, ethical standing, courage, ability, fairness, cool-headedness, consistency, and respect for the personality and opinion of subordinates, the commander vitally influences the entire condition of the brigade, especially the morale of units and command." Can you tell -- can you bring that down to a practical level? What does that mean, this personal conduct with all these things, "vitally influences the entire condition"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Perhaps the best I've heard it ever explained is the testimony of General Dannett during the Krstic trial, where he explained that command is a personal thing. Of all of the individuals in a particular unit, from platoon level to the very top, the individual temperament, qualities, moral courage, personality of the commander is a decisive factor in influencing the brigade, and not just the brigade but obviously in any unit; and, certainly, subordinates, when they're ably led like that, will often reflect the character -- the positive characteristics and qualities of their command. The JNA obviously recognised that as a component of their own leadership training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to know whether this is a personal conclusion drawn by this expert or is this something that he just conveys, I mean, the conclusions drawn by General Dannett. He's just said the best explanation was the one provided by General Dannett.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, what Madame Fauveau is asking you is whether you are adopting the same approach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe he said it far better than I could. He's hit it right on the button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that clear, Madame Fauveau? Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we will soon see documents, well, from the highest levels down to the lowest levels, including the brigade levels, where commanders are making reference to the enemy in derogatory terms, such as "Poturice," "Turks." Does that kind of conduct fit into this second paragraph, "through his personal conduct," et cetera, "influences the entire condition"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not working all day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know there's something wrong, but please be patient. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I object to that. That is not a question of military analysis or expertise, and it's simply Mr. McCloskey making a comment and requiring confirmation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I absolutely -- I'm sorry. I've been told to have both these on so people could hear me. But I absolutely disagree with that. This is a fundamental and important principle that has -- and maybe we should have it outside of the conduct of the witness, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want, we can do that. I think it's not difficult for us to decide, but if you wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have -- we have documents I'll refer to. I'm just asking Mr. Butler if those documents that have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you then wait until you make use of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this -- because I believe it's an unfounded objection, and this is a principle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's discuss it in the absence of the witness, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll soon call you back, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to explain yourself better, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I've explained myself well enough. I've held off on this objection as long as I could. Of course, it would not be a good indication of anybody's character if they used racially-pejorative terms. It's a matter of common sense that it's not a good example for a commander to set, and this is simply a comment by Mr. McCloskey seeking the confirmation of this witness. It's much of same as the one he asked earlier about whether mistreating your prisoners would lead to mistreatment of your prisoners by the other side. Of course, it would, but it's not something that requires a military analyst to tell us. This question goes nowhere. It isn't, in fact, a question. As I've said, it's just a comment, and it's just seeking this man's confirmation of it. I don't really want to say any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with counsel in that comments referring to the enemy in a -- in derogatory terms to one's troops is a particularly damaging principle that -- or conduct thing to do that filters down and can have extremely damaging effects. What I'm looking to, to determine, is whether or not this particular definition that talks about personal conduct vitally influencing the command has any relationship with that kind of conduct, as I would when I get to those documents, though you've seen many of them so far. Does this description of one's personal conduct have to do with one's -- things like the example I give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this phase, at this stage, we don't really see the need for this question, Mr. McCloskey. But then when you are, in due course, if at all, you are referring to specific documents and you may wish to -- you wish to ask questions to the witness, we'll consider each question on its own merits at that stage. But for the time being, I think we can safely proceed with your next question. Bring Mr. Butler in again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you tell us, in your experience, how important is it for a commander to lead by example, by positive example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the framework of my own military background, that is probably the key fundamental tenet of command and of leadership is that it's leadership by example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We'll get some actual examples of that a little later on, but right now let's go to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 699.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another manual that you have identified over the years. It's entitled "Manual for the Work of Commands and Staff," and it's describing under "Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to go to page 15, if we can, in the English, and it's B/C/S page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall this particular manual?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember what it is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: While the brigade regulations and other JNA regulations talk about and give some details with respect to how the command and staff processes should work in a properly-functioning unit, what this particular manual does is really gets into the minutiae and all of the technical details about all of the various forms of interrelationship between a commander and those officers who are part of a commander's staff, and its rules are applicable from the battalion all the way up into the highest levels of staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's go to page 15 in the English, and I don't -- we see paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says: "Command is a process function of control ..." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Command -- essentially, command or the action of command is how the individual exercises control over the functions of the unit. There are various ways it can be done, as the remainder of the paragraph points out, either by, you know, direct orders, broader guidance or directive, instructions, and a command act in effect being an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then we see, in number 14: "Coordination is a function of command (part of the process) and control coordinating various elements in the execution of the task that has been set. "Coordination ensures harmonious work within and among the commands and staff and other organs of control," and it goes on. What does that mean, in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In practical terms, within a particular staff, it recognises the fact that a staff may be organised in many certain ways, in the context of the former JNA, where you have assistant commanders of morale or political works at the time, assistant command for logistics, assistant for security, you have chiefs of intelligence and other staff bodies. Now, the issue of coordination is the fact that, well, staff officers and staff elements have their own specific responsibilities, that they are to work with an eye towards ensuring that their activities are properly coordinated with the ultimate goal of fulfilling and ensuring the commander's order and intent to make sure that, you know, the operations people, when they're designing a particular operations order or op plan, you have the logistics staff that is part of that entire process. You don't have a situation where different things are being done by different entities without coordination, I guess using the word again. Within a unit, it is also between other units you'll have coordination, where you'll have, for example, coordination between multiple brigades or multiple elements of multiple units for a senior commander. You can also have elements of coordination between the military and other political entities that would support the military; although, that would normally fall more along the lines of collaboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see "Cooperation," and it appears to define it in, I think, the term we're all familiar with, so I won't ask you about that, but that does get us to "Collaboration," which is the manner of regulating the relations between unit commands which engage in combat and control organs and other things. So how does collaboration differ from coordination and cooperation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Collaboration more accurately describes issues that involve elements of the army and non-military, or perhaps a better way to say it is non-army elements. For example, where you have a situation -- I mean, the term of "collaboration" is that the conditions of collaboration are set by superiors and that the units are expected to coordinate with each other within that framework. So when you have a situation, for example, where the army staff and the police staff have dictated, you know, how particular units can be used or under what parameters that they can be used, within the framework of those guidance from the senior commanders on both sides, the lower units are going to be expected to collaborate to ensure that they accomplish that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, "Verification." Again, we don't need to read that out. It's pretty clear. How important is verification in the process of exercising command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Verification is a key component of exercising command. A commander is ultimately responsible for the activities of his unit; and as part of the chain of command, his subordinates are expected to report back to him. As the commander, he is expected to verify, in case they don't report back, that his orders are being complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And these concepts of command, in your view, how well known are they to JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I can't foresee of a situation, particularly within the framework of the former JNA and the extent of its professional military development and education system, that officers who are essentially growing up within that environment are not going to know these issues. All officers are expected, within the various competencies, to know how to operate within this framework. It's a standard framework for the army. Many people who ultimately become commanders are individuals who will also have had extensive experience on staffs in order to be able to get as comprehensive a background of military knowledge as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we -- we'll get into some examples later, but just generally, do you see indications of Vinko Pandurevic and Mr. Borovcanin exercising these different concepts as they exercise command through the events that we look at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go to one particular area that you've talked about before, and that is the rules of the security organ. The Court has heard a fair amount about that, so I just want to touch on some of the basics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 407, this is a manual that's entitled "Rules of Service of Security Organs in the Armed Forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in 1984".

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's a document that has been established before in the trial, so I'm not going to ask you to authenticate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But I want to go to page 10 in the English, B/C/S page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll ask you to -- and under "Management," ask you to comment on paragraph 16: "The security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces in whose strength it is placed," et cetera. Can you just clearly tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It's a reflection of the earlier doctrine that within the -- within the framework of assistant commander for security, or security official, or assistant commander for logistics, or any of that nature, they are ultimately subordinate to the commanding officer of that unit. I mean, they are considered to be direct subordinates of him or her, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In comparison to that principle, let's look at 18 that talks about the security organs of the superior command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provide specialist administrative services for security organs in subordinate commands, et cetera. Can you distinguish for us the difference between a security organ being commanded by its commander and a security organ being provided specialist administrative services from the upper or superior security organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the -- the concept is that while the commander, of course, is the commander and the security officer or security official is his subordinate, it understands that the -- the reality that security, as well as other branches, are very technical branches and have a myriad of other responsibilities; and that in the conduct of those responsibilities, particularly with respect to security, counter-intelligence, or intelligence, or some things of that nature, that there is going to be guidance and technical support required by professionals in that particular field, senior intelligence and security officials. So there is a -- what is often referred to as a technical or management chain that runs along with but certainly doesn't supersede the command chain. So that particular technical support chain is how these particular officials would get additional guidance on, for example, counter-intelligence procedures and other security procedures that may have to be done, or they would get guidance with respect to threats that may be placed against particular military officers or information that has come through other operative channels that people may be attempting to target that unit for espionage or things of that nature. So the doctrine or, in their case, you know, the regulations, you know, recognise that concept and allow for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in any particular unit, be it brigade or corps or otherwise, who commands the military police unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The commander of the larger formation that that unit is subordinate to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what, generally, is the security officer's role, if any, in dealing with the military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As articulated by the regulations, the role of the security officer, with respect to the military police, is that he -- his role is to advise the commander on the most proper uses of that organisation and even to recommend what their function or what their tasks should be. The security officer recommends that and the detail necessary for the commander, and it is ultimately up to the commander to reject or to accept the recommendations of that officer and to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what unit is generally responsible for prisoners of war, in dealing with them and securing them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Insomuch as a unit echelon or what type of unit? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In a brigade, who would normally deal with detention issues, prisoner of war issues, as they are captured?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The front line units, the battalions and companies, generally would be the units to actually capture the prisoner in the first instance. However, according to the JNA regulations and the VRS instructions pertaining to those, the general procedure was that at the very earliest opportunity, these prisoners were to be turned over to the military police to ensure that they could be properly safeguarded and handled through the battlefield to the point where they were turned over to the individuals responsible for their -- for their detention on a longer period of level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've already talked a little bit about the relationship between the security officer and the military police, but does this include issues related to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I may go back to the relation, his role of the security officer, you said, Mr. Butler, that his role is to advise the commander. Does he not have anything to do directly with the police, the military police, himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once the commander, you know -- as the regulations go, once the commander accepts or modifies that guidance, most often it will be the security officer who will be instructed to implement it. In having his own direct contact with the military police, that security officer will be giving the direction and task to the military police commander as to how to accomplish that. In that particular context, the security officer, in given tasks like that, he's operating under the derived authority of the commander who approved the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is -- can that be comparable to other assistant commanders that have other tasks, like logistics or other situations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Regarding making -- what I'm asking, making proposals and then seeing that those proposals are carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Incumbent in the larger command and staff regulations, one of the primary purposes of the staff is to recommend, you know, and to develop courses of action for a commander, to recommend or propose -- to propose these lines of action to the commander. Once the commander makes the decision, it is usually those same staff officers who are going to be responsible for the implementation of it, turning the commander's guidance, direction, and verbal orders into the concrete and specific tasks necessary for the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look to one of the regulations on this that you've talked about in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is 65 ter 707. It's called "The Service Regulations of the SFRJ Armed Forces Military Police, 1985."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Coupled with the 19 -- coupled with the regulations we just talked about, these are the specific service regulations of the military police, armed forces military police applicable to the JNA, and referenced in all -- applicable to the VRS military police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 10 in the English and page 9 of the B/C/S that talks a little bit about the issues that we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 very simply means what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Specifically notes the officer in charge of the military unit and institution within whose establishment in the military police is placed or to which it is attached, commands and controls the military police. It reiterates the fact that the commander of a unit or installation, in our case let's use a brigade as an example, the brigade commander is the commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And, in paragraph 13, we can see that it says something very similar to what you just said, that the security officer makes -- controls the military police and makes suggestions to the officer in charge of the military unit and is responsible for their combat readiness and the performance of their tasks. So that -- I don't think I need to ask any more about that. You've answered that issue. But what I wanted to ask you about is it gets a little more detailed, and it says: "When controlling a military police unit, the officer in charge of the security body from paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties which the officers of arms of service of military units and institutions have in controlling the units of arms and services." Who are we talking about? Are we talking about the commander or the security officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In this passage, we are talking about the -- in this case, the assistant commanders for security in the same way having -- you know, having the same rights and authorities with respect to their function as assistant commanders for logistics or as a chief of intelligence might for their specific responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then the next paragraph talks about the traffic service. Does the security officer have any -- what's his responsibility regarding traffic military police issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Not particularly related to, you know, the traffic service; but, I mean, the recognition that under the rubric of the military police, there are a number of -- there are a wider variety of functions, many of them having to do with routine crime prevention and routine, in this case, traffic administration that, you know, are under the expertise of these assistant commanders. They're expected to -- to implement them. I mean, not implement them, but they're expected to be able to give the detailed technical advice and direction to accomplish these missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next paragraph, paragraph 14, identifies several examples of how the organisational unit controls the military police, from a specialist viewpoint. I won't go into that. I want to go into -- into some example documents relating to these regulations and ask you about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 2741, a document that came out in the Blagojevic case. This is a 24 October 1994 Main Staff instruction, as its entitled, "Command and Control over the Security and Intelligence Organs of the VRS." We can see that a couple of pages down it's under the name of Commander Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the first two numbered paragraphs. Number 1 seems to divide the work of the security and intelligence organs into two primary areas. Can you just briefly describe what those areas are, as you understand the regulations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The military police, of course, have a number of duties and responsibilities that are overseen, and what this particular instruction is indicating is that, you know, as a goal, again situation dependent, what those organs should be doing is spending 80 per cent of their time dealing with the intelligence, counter-intelligence, security rubric type of tasks; and then spend the remaining percentage of time doing all the other remaining tasks that fall under the mantra of the security officer, which would include things such as training, which would include things such as routine crime prevention activities. So, I mean, they're trying to find out that in an ideal situation, where they want to see the bulk of time and resources of this particular branch dedicated to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in paragraph 2, it says: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form part," which you've talked about at length so far, which I think is clear; and then there's, comma, "but with regard to professional activities, they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command." What does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Specifically, it delineates the responsibilities, effectively, you know, acknowledging that that security officer is a subordinate of the commander, but also reiterating the fact that in the conduct of some professional activities, particularly related to the counter-intelligence and security, that the commander does not have a role in either tasking or interfering with the work of the officer in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The next line says: "This indicates their full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and operative combinations, based on the authority set forth in the law." So is that the section you're referring to in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, it lays that out in further detail, but do you find that this instruction of 24 October changes the fundamental rules as they were used and set out in the JNA and used in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a quick question, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
