utterances.text: Does this rule relating to specialty also apply to another administrative commander -- I'm sorry, assistant commander; for example, logistics? If you could give me an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that in this particular case, I mean, this applies directly to the security officers and their branch, in recognition of their unique duties in counter-intelligence, which by definition, you know, have to be accomplished with a great degree of secrecy. One -- one can never say that maybe it's not the commander, himself, who may be the target of an investigation for security; and as a result, this is designed as a framework to ensure that an investigation or whatever investigative activity that needs to be accomplished can be done so without undue inference from the commander. On the other side of the situation, security officers and intelligence officers often run informants or operative agents or things of that nature whose identity must remain unknown for them to be able to do their work; and this ensures, as a mechanism, you know, going back to the laws and regulations on that type of operative work, that their identities can be kept from their commanders, even if they're ordered to be given to them, in order to continue the work. So I think it's unique to the security branch, where in the logistics branch or in the morale branch, you're not going to have those types of problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us another example of where the security branch would have -- would be different from some of the other branches; for example, correspondence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Normally -- and, again, there's -- as going into the work of the security branch, there are specifically regulated channels of communications by which information derived from intelligence work or security work or through operative contacts needs to travel to ensure its secrecy and the fact that it's not disseminated outside of established channels. So within that framework, each of the units having means of communication generally by courier in this particular context, where specialised instructions can be couriered from the superiors at the security branch to their subordinates, that won't necessarily come across the desk of the commander or the operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as an example of that, and I don't want to get into a lot of detail, but do you recall any -- any issue regarding this secrecy of correspondence that occurred between Drago Nikolic and Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There was some centre of dispute over whether or not the brigade commander, in this case Colonel Pandurevic, had the authority to make Drago Nikolic, his security officer, reveal operative-related information or security branch-related information. As I understand the testimony of a prior protected witness on this subject, and again from his previous testimony, there was some sense of dispute whether or not this material had to go through the commander or whether it could go separate of him; and my understanding is that a decision was reached, and Colonel Pandurevic was informed that these communications would not go through to him. They could go directly to the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, have you seen any examples of the work of the -- security officer's work with the military police as they relate to prisoners that would require this kind of secrecy that's for counter-intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. In fact, when you look at the documents that lay out the policy and the handling of procedures, those particular documents don't come through security officer channels. They are, in fact -- they come through command channels. The documents are signed not by security officers; they are signed by commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go through some examples of some security officer and others on some of these topics and get your viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3031, involving the -- it's a 29 January 1995 communication from the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, talking -- entitled "Changes in the Authorisation of VRS Security and Intelligence Support Delivery."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to read this entire document, but can you give us the gist of what Zivanovic is doing here? That should be on your tab --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I note specifically of interest paragraph 2, but take a moment to refresh your recollection on it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this case, depending upon the formation or organisation of a unit, whether it was a regular infantry brigade or whether it was a light infantry brigade, that differential depended on whether you had independent security and intelligence officers or whether you had one officer role to do both -- both details. In this particular order, they're reiterating, now, a prior order from the Main Staff, directing that as part of the unit formation. There would be a separation of functions between the security officers and the intelligence officers, again presumably to allow for each officer to focus more precisely on the tasks that they needed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in the -- was that necessary in the Zvornik Brigade at the time of -- in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In July of 1995, the Zvornik Brigade was not a light infantry brigade, so they already had separate branches for intelligence and security. So those functions had already been translated -- or had already been separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just to remind us, who was who? Who was intelligence and who was security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The security officer in this particular case would be Drago Nikolic, and the intelligence officer would be Captain Dusko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who, in this structure, was Captain Vukotic reporting to, his immediate supervisor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As the intelligence officer, his immediate supervisor would be It would be the Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At the time, it would be Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Drago Nikolic reported at the time to who? Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: His superior under the chain of command would have been Colonel Pandurevic. His superior, in terms of technical issues, would have been Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. How about the Bratunac Brigade, which was a light -- I think we heard evidence that it was a light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, pursuant to this, they did separate the functions. What happened in the case of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade was that for the month of late June and July of 1995, the officer designated as the intelligence officer was given an additional task to lead a company of Bratunac Brigade soldiers, who were deployed to the turn of a battle front area out of the brigade's area of operations. So while, in theory, you had the two separate functions, the reality was that the only officer left home to do both functions was, in fact, the assistant commander for security, Captain First Class Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if you could, we see in paragraph 4 here: "Security organs and intelligence organs shall exchange information of importance on a daily basis." Now, the Trial Chamber has heard about some intelligence -- the intelligence side and the security side, but could you give us just the brief -- the brief difference; and if there's a difference, why paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It recognises that there is a commonality of purpose for both specific organs and the fact that information obtained through intelligence channels may have importance to maintaining the overall security posture of the unit and that information obtained through security channels may have intelligence value, particularly with, you know, relationship to, you know, the interrogation of prisoners of war, or line-crossers, or individuals of that nature who may be interviewed or investigated by one organ or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in the next paragraphs, it points out that the obligations, in the sense of information, professional administration, and personal affairs, shall remain as pursuant to the Main Staff instruction 1820, and then all those numbers, 28 October. Now, I don't need you to compare all the numbers. I notice there's a date between the Mladic October 1994 date and this date; but to your understanding, what is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe it's a reference to the Main Staff order that we just discussed on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the -- while the date is different, the order numbers are identical, and it may be a typo. We'll check on that. All right. Now I want to go to a couple of examples of some normal communication of the security branch, the first one being one from Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, and it's 65 ter 3032.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 7 February 1995. It's to the commands of all these -- of all the Drina Corps brigades, and I notice the "5BVP." Can you tell us what "5BVP" is? That should be your tab 20, on the front page.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I only have the Serbo-Croatian version. I don't have the English one. I'll have to read it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: "5BVP" is the standard abbreviation that they use for the 5th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Each corps is a component of its organisational formation. It's supposed to have a military police battalion directly subordinate to the corps commander. In the case of the Drina Corps, the military police unit, while being called a battalion, actually numbered far less in size of personnel. I don't think it ever approached company strength. So, you know, it's called a battalion, but in reality we're talking about a unit of far less personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, again, I don't want to read this whole document out, but we can see that its entitled: "We have received a very urgent telegram from our superior command, obliging us to give short and clear responses with examples to these statements. "And then in the different statements, one is entitled "Command of the Military Police," "Level of Training," "Mobilisation," "Security Tasks for the Military Police," "The Use of the Military Police of the Muslim Army." So we have a security officer of the Drina Corps. What's he doing here and what's this about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I'm going to have to scroll -- if I could ask them to scroll down on this particular order. Thanks. This particular order is essentially Colonel Popovic asking the subordinate military police personnel, in the case the commanders not only of the brigade but of other companies, and platoons in some cases, to survey the types of jobs, roles, and functions that they're doing to provide information on what they think they should be doing as a component of their roles and responsibilities, and to provide any information of what their professional counterparts in the enemy forces, ABiH and even Croatian Army, are doing as a way of essentially surveying the general military police community and trying to determine whether or not the tasks that they are engaged in are, in fact, the tasks that, by regulation and doctrine, they should be carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, can you remind us, why is a security officer involved in this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, he is again the officer on the Drina Corps staff who, by position, should have the most detailed knowledge about the specific or technical issues that the military police not only are engaged in on a daily basis, but, by doctrine, what the military police's role should be in the armed forces as a matter of their training and as a matter of their functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a concern that the military police were being used improperly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of the -- one of the constant factors of the war, from the perspective of the Army of Republika Srpska, was that they did not have the required manpower to, you know, fully bring their own formations up to strength. As a result, one of the unfortunate side effects, from a position of VRS command, was that military police units were very often used as infantry forces to plug a place or a gap in the line or to deploy as a reserve force, because the commands did not have adequate manpower to use other designated infantry units. So instead of doing their police functions, which they of course received specialised training for and equipment, more often than not they were thrown in to performing strictly infantry functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and briefly did that happen in the Zvornik Brigade area on 13/14 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get into that in more detail when we -- when we get there. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another document by at that time Major Popovic, and it's 65 ter 196, dated 15 April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is again to the -- it says "to the command of" and then all the brigades, and as well as the 5th Engineer Battalion, and it says: "Intelligence and security organ heads." Now, can you tell, from the title of this document, whether this is the document that would have gone to the commands or if this may have been one of those more secretive documents? Is that even possible to tell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It's not a -- it's not a secret document, in the operative sense of the word. A document like this would have been routinely transmitted through the normal communication channels in most instances. It's not a particularly sensitive document;, but, of course it's directed to the intelligence and security organ heads as the relevant individuals who are in the position to have to execute this technical guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's entitled "Arrest and Detention of POWs and Other Persons," and then it says "Instruction." Now, first of all, can you tell us what, basically, this instruction is doing and how, if at all, does it fit into this -- the discussion of the rights and responsibilities, the duties and responsibilities of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe this particular document is a classic example of the technical guidance and direction that the superior security organ, you know, would be expected to provide to the lower security organs with respect to this issue. It notes the fact that they are receiving information that handling not only prisoners of war but handling individuals who are accused of regular criminal acts among the troops is being done in such a manner that it could potentially compromise the unit security. A good example of that is the notation, I believe, on the second page of the English translation that, you know, there -- some of these people are being segregated after they're captured and being held for a period of time in company or battalion command posts, where they're in a position to potentially overhear or learn about military operations or orders that the unit is carrying out, and, you know, notes the fact that at some point in time these individuals may be traded and that the information that they learn, as part of being captured in where they're held, may ultimately fall into the hands of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how does this fit together with your earlier discussion? For example, this says, on page 2, it says: "Instruction." Is that different than "Order"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is, but, I mean, this again -- it falls into the classic example of the type of technical guidance and direction that a security officer is within his purview to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's go to another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's also by this time Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic, dated 20 April 1995. 65 ter 3033. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, it says: "To the commands of the brigades." This time it gets into the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment. What's the 5th Mixed Artillery Regiment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, as part of its formation background, each course has a mixed artillery regiment or some corps had multiple ones. This is the unit that consolidated the artillery assets of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this -- this heading says: "Strictly for the chief of intelligence and security affairs." So what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This is a document that, when you read it in the context, would certainly qualify as an operative document that would not go through normal channels. I would presume - I don't know whether it did or not - but I presume that based on the content, it wouldn't go through normal channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you briefly summarise the content? I don't want to go into the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The content of this particular order outlines operative information that the army has received that their -- you know, after the 50th Session of the RCS National Assembly, that there is a plot or contract to assassinate General Mladic and potentially other senior members of the army. Having laid that out, it directs the security officers to take the necessary steps, within the confines of their responsibility, to, one, initiate investigations at all levels within their units to determine if they potentially have any information to add to this investigation, and, two, you know, when or if they become aware that some of these senior officers may be passing through or may be staying at that location, to ensure that they take the necessary steps to ensure the safety and security of the senior officers as they travel through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3014. It's dated 18 July 1995. We see a command stamp. In the English, it says "15," but I'm not really that concerned about the date. Again -- and I think we have another translation problem. This is not Second-Lieutenant Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another document that's entitled: "To the chiefs in the intelligence and security organs," entitled, "Dealing with reporter crews." What does this document basically do and how does it fit into your analysis of a security officer's job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The VRS, perhaps like most military institutions, tends to view the media as a potential security threat. This is, again, a classic example of the security officer exercising, you know, the authorities within his competence to -- in order to ensure that the media crews or outlets do not get information which could potentially be viewed as compromising the security of VRS units or operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does that fit into the 80 per cent counter-intelligence or the 20 per cent military police law enforcement work, or someplace else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I think this type of example falls firmly into the 80 per cent counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, that is -- those are my questions related to the security branch. I wanted to move on now to something that you said earlier on when you talked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If my colleague is moving on to another topic, I have a clarification I would like to see of something that came out of page 89, lines 33 and 34. I didn't do it before that. That's way back, and I wanted to let him finish that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 89?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 89, lines 33 and 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And on this occasion, the response of Mr. Butler was that this was a reference to "earlier doctrine," and I would just like to know what he meant by it. For clarification purposes, it might save a lot of time in cross-examination. Has there been new doctrine since then, or Why did he say "earlier doctrine"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, the question was you were being referred to document 65 ter 407, which is a manual entitled: "Rules of Service of Security Organs" in the Armed Forces of the Socialist -- SFRY, and particularly to a paragraph thereof or a part thereof which said: "The security organ is directly subordinate to the commanding officer of the command unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces, in whose strength it is placed," et cetera. Then you were asked: "Can you clearly tell us what that means?" Your answer was: "It is a reflection of the earlier doctrine that within the framework of assistant commander for security or security officials, or assistant commander for logistics, or any of that nature, they are ultimately subordinate to the commanding officer of that unit. I mean, they are considered to be direct subordinates of him or her, as the case may be." Mr. Bourgon is asking you to be more specific when you refer to "earlier doctrine" by explaining what you really meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I refer to the earlier doctrine, I believe the -- what he's looking for is the -- in this particular context that we're talking about, the 19 -- the 1984 JNA brigade rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to add further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I can take that up on cross-examination, but it's just because when he used the word "earlier," has there been a change? I think my colleague is as much interested as I am in getting an answer to this question, or has there been a change?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to elaborate this further or do you wish to move to the next topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he is means "discussed earlier," but I think it's going to -- if Mr. Butler reads the whole business, I mean, he discussed this earlier-discussed doctrine of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't try to explain yourself what he meant. If he wishes to add anything coming, he's perfectly capable of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's a very simple explanation, and I think this kind of interruption can be helpful, I agree, but it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But on the other hand, Mr. Bourgon waited until you had closed the chapter you were dealing with, so let's not make a mountain out of it. Yes, your next question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I better clarify that, if I could, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The doctrine, the security doctrine that's set forth in the rule on security, as it was stated, the commander of the unit, commander of the security, is there some earlier security doctrine that was different from the rule that you were talking about? I think that's what Mr. Bourgon is concerned about.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I think there were earlier security doctrines published by the JNA, but I've not reviewed them, so, I mean, I'm not talking about an earlier doctrine in that context. We reviewed the material from this particular date group because it was the most contemporary JNA doctrine related to these functions before the JNA ceased to exist as part of the war. So I don't mean to make the -- the claim that there is pre-1984 -- or pre-doctrine that I haven't talked about that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now I just want to ask you about -- you've earlier testified that the Ministry of Interior units were part of the armed forces in an imminent war or state of war, and I want to direct your attention to 65 ter 422, which is a law, entitled "The Law on the Implementation of the Law Internal Affairs during Imminent Threat of War or State of War."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's look at, I believe, it's page 9 in the English and page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's Article 4 that I'm -- that I believe you've referenced in the past, and can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It just reiterates what I indicated earlier. It's the background source that during a declared state of imminent threat of war or a state of war, that the Ministry of the Interior forces are considered to be a component part of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, under the command of the president as the commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And would that include what the Courts heard regarding the special police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They are a -- they are a component part of the Ministry of the Interior and would be covered under this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 12 of the English, of the same law. It's number 4, and it's page 4 in the B/C/S. This is the first article, and then we go on to some of the other articles on page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's entitled: "The Use of Police Units in Combat Operations," and I want to direct your attention in particular to Article 14, which states: "Police units assigned to combat operations by an order of the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces shall be resubordinated to the commander of the unit in whose zone of responsibility they are performing combat tasks." It goes on to say: "Police units shall be under the direct command of a commander who is a member of the Ministry of the Interior. During the time they are resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska, they shall retain their organisation and may not be split up or separated. "Police units resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska in a certain zone shall be used only for combat operations established in advance by the commander-in-chief or the Minister of the Interior." Then lastly: "In the zone in which they are carrying out combat operations, the commander to whom a police unit has been resubordinated shall provide logistic support for the police unit in the same way as the other units of the Army of Republika Srpska." Now, can you tell us, what is the significance of this law, actually, do -- to your case - or to your analysis? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, the first thing it indicates is that, you know, when you have a situation where the police are resubordinated to the military for the conduct of military operations, while the army has a great deal of latitude with respect to using the police, and previously in designated combat tasks, they don't have unlimited authority over police forces. For example, the army cannot relieve the police unit commander of command of his own troops, nor can they, now, for whatever expedient reason, essentially disband that unit and take those particular soldiers and move them wholesale into army formations. So it establishes, by law, limits to the issue of command that the military commanders can exercise over the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 29 November 1994. Were you aware of any issues or problems that were related to the enactment of this -- of this legislation or law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Towards the -- towards the end of 1994, particularly with respect to the situation in the far western portion of the Krajina, specifically the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps in the Bihac area, the military operations that were being conducted there were of such scope and intensity and the manpower was so poor that the army was having significant problems dealing with that situation. I believe that General Milavonovic [phoen] noted to some degree that one of the things that he had personally asked the president of the republic to implement was an imminent state of war, which would give the military additional powers and additional manpower assets, at least in that particular part of the country, in order to deal with the military threat. So concurrent with, you know, the army asking for these additional powers, there appears to be, from the legislative side of Republika Srpska, an effort to more finely codify what these additional powers and responsibilities meant, not only to the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior police, but in this particular Official Gazette, it is entirely comprised of laws for almost every branch of the government on how their activities will be regulated during the same time. So it sounds like somewhere towards the back part of 1994, the government, as it -- you know, the legislative and the executive bodies of the RS government, decided they needed to sit down and codify, under law, just what those differentials meant in each and every circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it's time now to object to these types of questions, Mr. President. The question that's put to the witness as to whether he is aware of any problems or issues, and then the witness goes into an interpretation of a situation that took place in 1994, without quoting any documents, without quoting any specific source, and he talks about his knowledge of what happened in 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can cross-examine him on that. I mean, the purpose of the question was to try and make some sense of the document that the witness is being shown in relation to a particular period in time. So if you have problems or questions to put, put them on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is not qualified to talk about what happened in 1994, and he's not qualified to give interpretation of problems of a legislative nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is being asked why it is, in this particular period in 1994, that this document emerges from the VRS. So let's proceed, please. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We're joining the objection, and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the objection has already been decided, Mr. Ostojic. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will only add one other thing, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we better stay by the book, by the rules. If an objection has already been decided, you sit down. It's over. If you have a fresh objection, we will deal with it, but not the same objection. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, let's go to a document that's 65 ter 57. This is a document that is entitled: "Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, Cabinet of the Minister," dated 10 July 1995, to various police commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, Mr. Butler, does this -- well, first of all, can you just briefly outline what -- and we're going to get into this in more detail now, but I just want to know: Is there, in your view, a relationship between this document and the previous law you just went over?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe this is a -- this is an excellent example of just how that law was manifested in the practical reality on the ground when it came to these situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you point to a couple of examples in this document to back that up?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It notices that it was the -- pursuant to the order of the supreme commander of the RS, reiterating President Karadzic's authority as the supreme commander to give ut this order. It reiterates -- you know, it designates a commander for the police units. It regulates the issue with respect to once a unit arrives, it is obliged to make contact with the corps chief of staff, General Krstic. So, in a sense, it regulates -- you know, or it manifests itself on the law and the requirements of the law and how this is done, and further reiterates the fact that once the particular unit or this amalgamations of unit gets to the destination is to put itself at the direction of General Krstic, report to him for further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, when it says "obliged to make contact with Corps Chief of Staff General Krstic," does that imply any kind of command relationship between the MUP forces and General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I read it to be as such, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. One more document on this topic, a short document. Let's go to Exhibit it looks like 4D00087, a 15 July document from the Drina Corps Command to the Main Staff, requesting food provisions for a MUP unit monitoring the Srebrenica and Bratunac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what this is and whether it fits that law you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't think we went over this component verbally; but as a component of that, when these forces fall under the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We haven't received the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecutor repeat the sentence he just read from this document, the whole sentence, please, because half of the sentence may alter the meaning of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have time for that today because it's 4.30, or shall we adjourn? We adjourn until tomorrow. Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Mr. Butler, we are adjourning today. Before we wind up, I wish to thank you all for having made yourself available this afternoon to recover, recoup some of the time we lost this morning, not due to anybody's fault. In particular, I also wish to thank the interpreters, the technicians, the reporters, and the rest of the staff that have been working hard. Thank you.
